title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
text: English | 한글

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
section: Stress is more than force divided by area
text:
Stress is more than force divided by area
One of the first equations encountered in mechanics of materials is
\[
\sigma = \frac{F}{A}.
\]
This equation is useful, but it can also leave an incomplete picture of what stress really means.
At a point inside a three-dimensional body, there is no single stress value that can describe the forces acting across every possible internal surface.
To understand stress properly, we should begin not with the stress tensor itself, but with a simple physical operation:
Imagine cutting the body.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
text:
Make an internal cut
Consider a point \(P\) inside a body.
Imagine a small internal surface passing through \(P\). Let its area be \(\Delta S\) and let its orientation be specified by the unit normal vector \(\mathbf n\).
The material on one side of the cut exerts a force \(\Delta \mathbf F\) on the material on the other side.
As the surface becomes infinitesimally small, we define the traction vector
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}(P)
=
\lim_{\Delta S\rightarrow 0}
\frac{\Delta \mathbf F}{\Delta S}.
\]



Internal cut and traction vector. The two sides of the internal surface exert equal and opposite tractions.


Traction therefore represents force per unit area acting across an oriented internal surface.
The word oriented is important.
If we examine the same internal interface from the opposite side, the outward normal changes from \(\mathbf n\) to \(-\mathbf n\). Local equilibrium requires
\[
\mathbf t^{(-\mathbf n)}
=
-\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}.
\]
This is simply action and reaction expressed locally.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
section: The same point, but a different cut
text:
The same point, but a different cut
Now keep the material point \(P\) fixed, but change the orientation of the imaginary cutting plane.
The traction vector changes.



Different internal surfaces passing through the same point generally have different traction vectors.


This observation is fundamental.
The vector
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
\]
is not associated with the point \(P\) alone. It is associated with the pair
\[
(P,\mathbf n).
\]
At the same material point, different surface orientations generally produce different traction vectors.
This raises the central question:

Can we find one object at \(P\) that generates the traction vector for every possible surface orientation?

In other words, can we find a local rule
\[
\mathbf n
\longmapsto
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}?
\]
That object is the Cauchy stress tensor.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
text:
Start with three coordinate planes
Before considering every possible orientation, consider three particular surfaces through the point.
Let their outward normals be the Cartesian basis vectors
\[
\mathbf e_1,\qquad
\mathbf e_2,\qquad
\mathbf e_3.
\]
The corresponding traction vectors are
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_1)},\qquad
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_2)},\qquad
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_3)}.
\]



A stress state represented by the traction vectors acting on three coordinate-aligned surfaces.


Each traction vector has three Cartesian components.
Using the convention
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_j)}
=
\sigma_{1j}\mathbf e_1
+
\sigma_{2j}\mathbf e_2
+
\sigma_{3j}\mathbf e_3,
\]
the three traction vectors can be assembled as the columns of a matrix.
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
| & | & |\\
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_1)}
&
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_2)}
&
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_3)}
\\
| & | & |
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Thus,
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\sigma_{11} & \sigma_{12} & \sigma_{13}\\
\sigma_{21} & \sigma_{22} & \sigma_{23}\\
\sigma_{31} & \sigma_{32} & \sigma_{33}
\end{bmatrix}.
\]
Here,
\[
\sigma_{ij}
\]
is the component in the \(\mathbf e_i\) direction of the traction acting on the surface whose normal is \(\mathbf e_j\).
Therefore,

\(i=j\): normal stress component,
\(i\ne j\): shear stress component.

The nine components describe the three traction vectors acting on the three coordinate planes.
But this leads to another question.
We know the tractions on three particular planes. How can we determine the traction on a plane having an arbitrary orientation?
The answer comes from equilibrium.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
text:
Cauchy’s tetrahedron
Consider an infinitesimal tetrahedron surrounding the material point.
Its oblique face has area \(dA\) and outward unit normal
\[
\mathbf n
=
n_1\mathbf e_1
+
n_2\mathbf e_2
+
n_3\mathbf e_3.
\]
The other three faces are aligned with the coordinate planes and have outward normals
\[
-\mathbf e_1,\qquad
-\mathbf e_2,\qquad
-\mathbf e_3.
\]



Cauchy’s tetrahedron. Equilibrium relates the traction on an arbitrarily oriented surface to the tractions on the three coordinate planes.


From the geometry of the tetrahedron, the areas of the three coordinate faces are
\[
dA_1=n_1dA,
\]
\[
dA_2=n_2dA,
\]
and
\[
dA_3=n_3dA.
\]
Now apply equilibrium.
For a tetrahedron with characteristic dimension \(h\), the surface forces are of order
\[
O(h^2),
\]
whereas body forces and inertia are of order
\[
O(h^3).
\]
After dividing the equilibrium equation by \(dA\) and letting \(h\rightarrow0\), the surface-force balance becomes
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}dA
+
\mathbf t^{(-\mathbf e_1)}dA_1
+
\mathbf t^{(-\mathbf e_2)}dA_2
+
\mathbf t^{(-\mathbf e_3)}dA_3
=
0.
\]
Using the action–reaction relation
\[
\mathbf t^{(-\mathbf m)}
=
-\mathbf t^{(\mathbf m)}
\]
and the geometric relations
\[
dA_i=n_i dA,
\]
we obtain
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
=
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_1)}n_1
+
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_2)}n_2
+
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_3)}n_3.
\]
This is the crucial result.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
text:
Cauchy’s stress formula
Recall that
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_1)},\qquad
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_2)},\qquad
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf e_3)}
\]
are precisely the three columns of the stress tensor.
Therefore,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf n
}
\]
or, in component notation,
\[
t_i^{(\mathbf n)}
=
\sigma_{ij}n_j,
\qquad i,j=1,2,3.
\]
This is Cauchy’s stress formula.
It answers the question posed earlier.
At a given material point, the Cauchy stress tensor is the operator that determines the traction vector acting on any oriented surface through that point.
In this sense,
\[
\boxed{
\text{surface orientation}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\text{traction vector}
}
\]
is the essential meaning of the stress tensor.
More explicitly,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf n
\quad\xrightarrow{\;\boldsymbol{\sigma}\;}
\quad
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
}
\]
The stress tensor is therefore much more than a \(3\times3\) collection of stress components.
It is a linear mapping from the orientation of an internal surface to the traction acting on that surface.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
section: Normal and shear stresses on an arbitrary plane
text:
Normal and shear stresses on an arbitrary plane
Once \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\) is known, the traction vector on a surface with unit normal \(\mathbf n\) follows immediately:
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf n.
\]
We can now decompose this traction into normal and tangential parts.
The normal stress on the oriented surface is
\[
\sigma_n
=
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}\cdot\mathbf n.
\]
Using Cauchy’s stress formula,
\[
\boxed{
\sigma_n
=
\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf n
}
\]
The tangential or shear traction is then
\[
\boldsymbol{\tau}
=
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
-
\sigma_n\mathbf n,
\]
or
\[
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\tau}
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf n
-
(\mathbf n\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf n)\mathbf n
}
\]
Thus, normal stress and shear stress on an arbitrary plane are not separate stress quantities that must be independently specified.
They are simply the normal and tangential components of the traction vector generated by the stress tensor for that particular surface orientation.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
section: What does the stress tensor really represent?
text:
What does the stress tensor really represent?
It is tempting to identify the stress tensor with its nine Cartesian components,
\[
\sigma_{11},\sigma_{12},\ldots,\sigma_{33}.
\]
But those numbers are the components of the tensor in a chosen coordinate system.
The deeper physical object is the rule that determines how internal force is transmitted across an arbitrary oriented surface.
At a material point,
\[
\boxed{
\text{stress tensor}
=
\text{local rule: surface orientation}
\rightarrow
\text{traction vector}
}
\]
This interpretation makes the meaning of a second-order tensor much less mysterious.
We do not introduce the stress tensor simply because three-dimensional mechanics requires nine numbers.
We introduce it because the internal force transmitted across a surface depends on the orientation of that surface, and a single mathematical object is needed to describe that dependence.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
text:
Connection to the Z Diagram
This interpretation also clarifies one of the fundamental connections in the Z Diagram:
\[
F
\longleftrightarrow
\sigma.
\]
At the structural scale, loading and equilibrium are often described in terms of forces.
At the material-point scale, internal force transmission is described by traction and the stress tensor.
The connection between these descriptions is equilibrium.
Cauchy’s tetrahedron provides a particularly clear local demonstration of this principle.
Starting from the equilibrium of forces acting on an infinitesimal body, we arrive at
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf n.
\]
The stress tensor can therefore be understood as the local representation of internal force transmission within a continuum.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
text:
Watch the lecture
This topic is also discussed in my Mechanics of Materials lecture.

title: What Is a Stress Tensor, Really?
text:
Takeaway
If there is one idea to remember, it is not merely the formula
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf n.
\]
Instead, remember how we arrived at it.
Make an internal cut.
The cut exposes a traction vector.
Change the orientation of the cut, and the traction changes.
The three coordinate-plane tractions define the components of the stress tensor.
Equilibrium of Cauchy’s tetrahedron then shows that this one tensor generates the traction vector on every possible oriented surface:
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf n
}
\]
That is what the stress tensor really represents.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
text: English | 한글

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
text:
From stress to strain
In the previous article, we asked what the stress tensor really represents.
Starting from an imaginary internal cut, we found that the Cauchy stress tensor provides the local mapping
\[
\mathbf n
\quad\xrightarrow{\;\boldsymbol{\sigma}\;}
\quad
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)},
\]
or
\[
\mathbf t^{(\mathbf n)}
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot \mathbf n.
\]
The stress tensor therefore tells us how internal force is transmitted across an arbitrarily oriented surface.
But this immediately raises another question.
What deformation measure naturally pairs with stress when mechanical work is considered?
We often write the internal virtual work as
\[
\delta W_{\mathrm{int}}
=
\int_\Omega
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
\,dV.
\]
Here and throughout this article, the tensor-operation symbols are written explicitly when they help distinguish the operation:
\[
\otimes:\;\text{tensor product (no contraction)},
\qquad
\cdot:\;\text{single contraction},
\qquad
::\;\text{double contraction}.
\]
Thus \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf n\) is a single contraction, whereas \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}:\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) is a double contraction. The symbols are a notation convention used here for clarity; the underlying operation is best checked from the repeated and free indices.
This formula is fundamental in solid mechanics and finite element analysis.
But why does the strain tensor \(\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}\) appear here?
Why not simply the displacement gradient \(\nabla\mathbf u\)?
The answer follows naturally from traction work, equilibrium, and the symmetry of the stress tensor.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
text:
Start from traction work
Consider a body occupying a region \(\Omega\) with boundary \(\partial\Omega\).
Let \(\mathbf t\) denote the traction acting on the boundary and \(\delta\mathbf u\) an admissible virtual displacement.
The virtual work done by the surface tractions is
\[
\delta W_t
=
\int_{\partial\Omega}
\mathbf t\cdot\delta\mathbf u
\,dA.
\]
From Cauchy’s traction law,
\[
\mathbf t
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot \mathbf n,
\]
where \(\mathbf n\) is the outward unit normal to the boundary.
Therefore,
\[
\delta W_t
=
\int_{\partial\Omega}
(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot \mathbf n)
\cdot
\delta\mathbf u
\,dA.
\]
This is where the result of the previous stress-tensor discussion becomes the starting point of the present one.
We now want to transform this boundary work into a quantity defined throughout the volume.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
section: From the boundary to the volume
text:
From the boundary to the volume
Using indicial notation,
\[
\delta W_t
=
\int_{\partial\Omega}
\sigma_{ij}n_j\delta u_i
\,dA.
\]
Applying the divergence theorem gives
\[
\delta W_t
=
\int_\Omega
(\sigma_{ij}\delta u_i)_{,j}
\,dV.
\]
Expanding the derivative,
\[
\delta W_t
=
\int_\Omega
\sigma_{ij,j}\delta u_i
\,dV
+
\int_\Omega
\sigma_{ij}\delta u_{i,j}
\,dV.
\]
Two terms have appeared.
The first involves the divergence of stress.
The second involves the displacement gradient.
Equilibrium tells us what to do with the first.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
text:
Equilibrium removes the body-force contribution
The local equilibrium equation is
\[
\sigma_{ij,j}+b_i=0,
\]
where \(b_i\) denotes the body force per unit volume.
Thus,
\[
\sigma_{ij,j}
=
-b_i.
\]
Substituting into the traction-work expression,
\[
\delta W_t
=
-
\int_\Omega
b_i\delta u_i
\,dV
+
\int_\Omega
\sigma_{ij}\delta u_{i,j}
\,dV.
\]
The total external virtual work includes both surface tractions and body forces:
\[
\delta W_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
\delta W_t
+
\int_\Omega
b_i\delta u_i
\,dV.
\]
The body-force terms cancel, leaving
\[
\boxed{
\delta W_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
\int_\Omega
\sigma_{ij}\delta u_{i,j}
\,dV
}
\]
or, in tensor notation,
\[
\boxed{
\delta W_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
\int_\Omega
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\nabla\mathbf u
\,dV
}
\]
This result is important.
Starting from forces acting on the boundary and applying equilibrium, we arrive naturally at a volume integral involving stress and the displacement gradient.
But we have not yet obtained the strain tensor.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
section: The displacement gradient contains two different motions
text:
The displacement gradient contains two different motions
The displacement gradient can be decomposed into symmetric and antisymmetric parts:
\[
\delta u_{i,j}
=
\delta\varepsilon_{ij}
+
\delta\omega_{ij},
\]
where
\[
\delta\varepsilon_{ij}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left(
\delta u_{i,j}
+
\delta u_{j,i}
\right)
\]
and
\[
\delta\omega_{ij}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left(
\delta u_{i,j}
-
\delta u_{j,i}
\right).
\]
In tensor form,
\[
\delta\nabla\mathbf u
=
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
+
\delta\boldsymbol{\omega}.
\]
The symmetric part,
\[
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left(
\nabla\mathbf u
+
\nabla\mathbf u^T
\right),
}
\]
is the familiar small-strain tensor.
The antisymmetric part,
\[
\boldsymbol{\omega}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left(
\nabla\mathbf u
-
\nabla\mathbf u^T
\right),
\]
represents infinitesimal rotation.
The question is now very precise:
Which part of the displacement gradient performs internal work against the stress tensor?

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
section: Why rotation disappears from the work
text:
Why rotation disappears from the work
Substitute the decomposition into the work expression:
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\nabla\mathbf u
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
+
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\omega}.
\]
For the classical Cauchy continuum, the stress tensor is symmetric:
\[
\sigma_{ij}
=
\sigma_{ji}.
\]
Meanwhile, the infinitesimal rotation tensor is antisymmetric:
\[
\delta\omega_{ij}
=
-\delta\omega_{ji}.
\]
The double contraction of a symmetric tensor with an antisymmetric tensor vanishes:
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\omega}
=
0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\nabla\mathbf u
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
\delta W_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
\int_\Omega
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
\,dV
}
\]
and, under equilibrium, this is identified with the internal virtual work:
\[
\boxed{
\delta W_{\mathrm{int}}
=
\int_\Omega
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
\,dV.
}
\]
Now the strain tensor has appeared.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
section: Why does the strain tensor appear?
text:
Why does the strain tensor appear?
This derivation gives a physical answer.
We did not begin by defining the strain tensor and then searching for a use for it.
Instead, we began with the work done by physical tractions.
Through Cauchy’s traction law, the divergence theorem, and equilibrium, the boundary work became
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\nabla\mathbf u.
\]
The displacement gradient contains both deformation and rotation.
But because the Cauchy stress tensor is symmetric, the rotational part performs no work:
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\omega}
=
0.
\]
What remains is the symmetric part:
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
\]
So the small-strain tensor
\[
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
=
\frac12
\left(
\nabla\mathbf u+\nabla\mathbf u^T
\right)
}
\]
emerges naturally as the deformation measure that is work-conjugate to the Cauchy stress tensor in the small-strain formulation.
This is one reason the strain tensor occupies such a fundamental position in mechanics.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
section: From internal work to strain energy
text:
From internal work to strain energy
The incremental internal work density is
\[
dU
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
d\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
\]
For linear elastic loading,
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}
=
\mathbb C:\boldsymbol{\varepsilon},
\]
where \(\mathbb C\) is the fourth-order elasticity tensor.
The strain-energy density becomes
\[
U
=
\int
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
d\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
\]
For linear elasticity,
\[
\boxed{
U
=
\frac12
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
}
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\boxed{
U
=
\frac12
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}:
\mathbb C:
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
}
\]
Stress and strain are therefore not merely two quantities related by a constitutive equation.
They form an energy-conjugate pair.
Their contraction has the meaning of work or energy per unit volume.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
text:
Connection to the Z Diagram
This gives a deeper interpretation of the central part of the Z Diagram:
\[
F
\longleftrightarrow
\sigma
\longleftrightarrow
\varepsilon
\longleftrightarrow
u.
\]
The previous article concentrated on
\[
F
\longleftrightarrow
\sigma,
\]
showing how equilibrium connects structural forces with the local stress state.
The present derivation concentrates on
\[
\boxed{
\sigma
\longleftrightarrow
\varepsilon.
}
\]
The connection is fundamentally energetic:
\[
dU
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
d\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
\]
At the material-point scale, stress and strain are energy-conjugate quantities.
At the structural scale, force and displacement form the corresponding work pair.
Schematically,
\[
\boxed{
\mathbf F\cdot d\mathbf u
\quad\longleftrightarrow\quad
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
d\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
}
\]
or, for the whole body,
\[
dW_{\mathrm{external}}
=
\int_\Omega
dW_{\mathrm{internal}}.
\]
This is one of the reasons energy provides such a powerful way of connecting the different quantities appearing in structural mechanics.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
text:
Beyond small strain
The same idea continues into finite-deformation mechanics, but the appropriate deformation measure depends on the configuration being used.

Current configuration
Let the deformed body occupy \(\Omega_t\).
The external power due to surface traction is
\[
P_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
\int_{\partial\Omega_t}
\mathbf t\cdot\mathbf v
\,da.
\]
Using Cauchy’s traction law and the divergence theorem gives
\[
P_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
\int_{\Omega_t}
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\nabla\mathbf v
\,dv.
\]
The velocity gradient can be decomposed as
\[
\nabla\mathbf v
=
\mathbf d+\mathbf w,
\]
where
\[
\mathbf d
=
\frac12
\left(
\nabla\mathbf v+\nabla\mathbf v^T
\right)
\]
is the rate-of-deformation tensor and
\[
\mathbf w
=
\frac12
\left(
\nabla\mathbf v-\nabla\mathbf v^T
\right)
\]
is the spin tensor.
Again, because
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}^T,
\]
we have
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:\mathbf w=0.
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
P_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
\int_{\Omega_t}
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:\mathbf d
\,dv.
}
\]
The Cauchy stress \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\) and the rate-of-deformation tensor \(\mathbf d\) form the corresponding power-conjugate pair in the current configuration.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
text:
Reference configuration
For finite deformation, introduce the deformation gradient
\[
\mathbf F
=
\frac{\partial\mathbf x}{\partial\mathbf X}
\]
and
\[
J=\det\mathbf F.
\]
The First Piola–Kirchhoff stress is
\[
\mathbf P
=
J\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf F^{-T}.
\]
The dot is shown explicitly here because \(\boldsymbol{\sigma}\cdot\mathbf F^{-T}\) is a single contraction between two second-order tensors. In matrix notation the same operation is often written simply as \(J\boldsymbol{\sigma}\mathbf F^{-T}\).
The power expression referred to the reference configuration can be written as
\[
\boxed{
P_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
\int_{\Omega_0}
\mathbf P:\dot{\mathbf F}
\,dV.
}
\]
Thus,
\[
\mathbf P
\quad\text{and}\quad
\dot{\mathbf F}
\]
form another work-conjugate pair.
Alternatively, define the Green–Lagrange strain
\[
\mathbf E
=
\frac12
\left(
\mathbf F^T\cdot\mathbf F-\mathbf I
\right).
\]
Its work-conjugate stress is the Second Piola–Kirchhoff stress \(\mathbf S\), giving
\[
\boxed{
P_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
\int_{\Omega_0}
\mathbf S:\dot{\mathbf E}
\,dV.
}
\]
So the particular stress and strain measures change with the formulation, but the underlying requirement remains the same:
the stress and deformation measures must form a consistent work-conjugate pair.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
text:
Watch the lecture
This derivation is also discussed in my Mechanics of Materials lecture.

title: Where Does the Strain Tensor Appear?
text:
Takeaway
Why does the strain tensor appear in mechanics?
Start from the work of surface tractions:
\[
\mathbf t\cdot\delta\mathbf u.
\]
Use Cauchy’s traction law, equilibrium, and the divergence theorem, and the corresponding volume quantity becomes
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\nabla\mathbf u.
\]
Then decompose the displacement gradient:
\[
\delta\nabla\mathbf u
=
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
+
\delta\boldsymbol{\omega}.
\]
Because stress is symmetric,
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\omega}
=
0.
\]
What remains is
\[
\boxed{
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
}
\]
Thus the strain tensor is not merely a convenient symmetrization of the displacement gradient.
It emerges naturally from the mechanics of internal work.
And this leads to one of the central energy relationships in solid mechanics:
\[
\boxed{
dU
=
\boldsymbol{\sigma}:
d\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}.
}
\]

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
text:
English | 한글
A discussion about continuing education for engineers can easily become a discussion about hours, approved courses, training providers, and compliance.
Those details matter. But they are not the first question.
The first question is more fundamental:
What kind of civil engineer are we trying to develop?
I returned to this question while preparing for a February 3 seminar in Korea on the education and training system for construction engineers. The seminar focused on real weaknesses in the current system: duplicated content, limited recognition of external learning, insufficient connection to practice, and long gaps in professional development after initial training.
Yet these problems point to something larger than the design of a continuing-education scheme.
If we define the profession too narrowly, we will also define its education too narrowly.
A civil engineer is not simply a construction engineer who needs periodic construction training. Civil engineering is concerned with the infrastructure systems on which society depends: how they are conceived, analyzed, designed, constructed, operated, maintained, adapted, and eventually renewed.
Once the profession is viewed in that broader way, university education and continuing professional development are no longer separate problems. They become different stages of the same process.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: Civil engineering is broader than construction engineering
text:
Civil engineering is broader than construction engineering
Construction is essential to civil engineering. A bridge that cannot be built is not a successful bridge design.
But civil engineering and construction engineering are not synonymous.
The distinction is visible even in formal accreditation criteria. ABET maintains separate program criteria for Civil and Similarly Named Engineering Programs and for Construction and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.
The current civil engineering criteria include mathematics through differential equations, probability and statistics, physics, chemistry, computing or data science, engineering mechanics, materials science, numerical methods, sustainability, risk, resilience, design, ethics, and complex engineering problems across at least four civil engineering specialty areas.
The construction engineering criteria, by comparison, focus more directly on construction methods, materials, equipment, planning, scheduling, safety, cost analysis, and the analysis and design of construction processes and systems.
Both are engineering. Both are important. But they are not the same educational domain.
This distinction matters because civil engineering itself is expanding.
Civil engineers work with structures and soils, water and transportation, environmental systems and construction. Increasingly, they also work with renewable energy infrastructure, offshore systems, climate adaptation and resilience, decarbonization, sensing, digital twins, data, and artificial intelligence.
These should not simply be treated as new boxes to add beside the traditional subdisciplines.
The engineering problems themselves are changing.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: How much can a university curriculum contain?
text:
How much can a university curriculum contain?
A broader profession creates an educational problem.
We cannot respond to every new development by adding another course.
AI becomes important, so we add an AI course. Offshore wind expands, so we add an offshore wind course. Climate adaptation becomes urgent, so we add another course. This process has no natural end.
Students may eventually encounter many subjects without developing enough depth to reason through an unfamiliar engineering problem.
The opposite approach is also inadequate. If structural, geotechnical, hydraulic, environmental, transportation, and construction engineering remain isolated educational silos, students may miss the system-level connections that define real infrastructure problems.
I therefore see three requirements for university civil engineering education:
deep fundamentals, structured breadth, and professional depth.
Mathematics, physics, mechanics, materials, fluids, probability, and computation are not merely early-year hurdles. They are durable tools for reasoning when a new problem does not look like one in a textbook.
Students also need a map of the broader civil infrastructure system. And within that map, they need enough depth in at least one area to solve real engineering problems rather than merely recognize terminology.
Civil engineering has always required both breadth and depth. The challenge is to make the relationship between them explicit.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: AI makes fundamentals more important, not less
text:
AI makes fundamentals more important, not less
If AI can perform calculations, generate code, search standards, and draft technical reports, why should students still study mechanics and mathematics deeply?
Because as the cost of producing an answer falls, the value of judging that answer rises.
An AI system may generate a finite element model. But are the boundary conditions physically meaningful?
Is the load path plausible?
Is a stress concentration a structural mechanism or a numerical artifact?
Does the code provision retrieved by the system actually apply to the structure and limit state being considered?
Software literacy alone cannot answer these questions.
They require mechanics, physics, materials knowledge, mathematical reasoning, and engineering judgment.
AI literacy and fundamentals are therefore not competing educational priorities.
The more readily engineers can generate answers, the more important it becomes to understand why an answer makes engineering sense.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: Graduation is not the end of civil engineering education

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: When continuing education becomes a training market
text:
When continuing education becomes a training market
The Korean seminar that prompted this article concerned a statutory education and training system for construction engineers.
Such systems have legitimate purposes. Safety requirements change. Regulations change. Engineers need opportunities to maintain and extend their competence.
But a mature mandatory-training system can develop its own institutional logic.
There are approved providers, approved curricula, required hours, administrative records, and a market built around supplying those hours.
The danger is not that a training market exists. The danger is that maintaining the training system becomes more important than developing the engineer.
Then providers tend to supply familiar courses, engineers focus on satisfying required hours, and government focuses on verifying completion.
The question gradually changes from

What does this engineer need to learn next?

into

Has this engineer completed the required training?

Those are not equivalent questions.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: Managing training hours is not managing engineering competence
text:
Managing training hours is not managing engineering competence
Hours are easy to count.
Competence is not.
Consider an engineer who encounters an unfamiliar problem in a project, studies technical papers, learns a new analysis method, reviews standards, discusses the problem with specialists, and applies the new knowledge successfully.
Has that engineer developed professionally?
Almost certainly.
But a system organized primarily around approved classroom hours may have difficulty recognizing that development.
This is why Continuing Professional Development, or CPD, is a more useful concept than continuing education alone.
The distinction is important:
managing educational attendance is not the same as managing professional competence.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: What can be learned from international CPD systems?
text:
What can be learned from international CPD systems?
International systems should not be reduced to a comparison of required hours.
The more interesting question is what they recognize as professional development and who is expected to take responsibility for it.
Engineers Australia requires Chartered engineers and engineers on the National Engineering Register to complete 150 hours of CPD over three years. Yet its conception of CPD is much broader than attendance at formal courses. Recognized activities include tertiary study, short courses, workshops, seminars, technical meetings, workplace learning that extends competence, private study, service to the engineering profession, preparation and presentation of technical material, and other structured activities. Engineering academics must also demonstrate at least 40 hours of industry involvement over three years.
This is significant. Reviewing technical publications, mentoring, participating in standards activities, studying technical literature, and developing new knowledge in practice can all contribute to professional development when they genuinely extend competence.
ASCE takes a different institutional approach but reaches a related conclusion about the need for continuing competence. Its current policy supports at least 15 documented professional development hours per year, including ethics training, as a condition for maintaining licensed Professional Engineer status. The stated reason is straightforward: practicing civil engineers must remain current with advances in technology, understanding of the world, and societal expectations.
The lesson is not that one national model should simply be copied.
Some systems prescribe hours. Others place greater emphasis on individually planned development. Professional and licensing bodies still audit, document, or regulate important requirements.
The deeper lesson is this:
professional development is broader than consuming courses.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: Move the center from the provider to the engineer
text:
Move the center from the provider to the engineer
A provider-centered system asks:

What courses should we offer?

A professional-development system starts with a different question:

What does this engineer need to learn to become a better engineer?

The difference is subtle in wording but fundamental in system design.
In the first question, the provider is the principal actor.
In the second, the engineer is.
Government still has an important role. Safety, ethics, public responsibility, and minimum professional requirements cannot simply be left to personal preference.
But government does not need to prescribe every useful learning activity. Its role can shift toward defining essential professional expectations, ensuring credible records and quality, and verifying that engineers continue to develop competence appropriate to their responsibilities.
Training providers then compete not merely to sell recognized hours but to provide knowledge that engineers actually need.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: Professional societies should connect knowledge producers and knowledge users
text:
Professional societies should connect knowledge producers and knowledge users
This change also suggests a different role for professional societies.
A society should not simply become another training vendor in an established mandatory-education market.
Its greatest assets are not classrooms.
They are people and knowledge.
Universities produce research. Design firms and construction sites accumulate experience. Failures sometimes produce particularly expensive knowledge. Codes evolve. New materials, methods, and computational technologies emerge.
Professional societies bring together many of the people who create, test, and interpret that knowledge.
Practicing engineers, meanwhile, encounter problems that require it.
The role of the professional society can therefore be understood as a connection:
\[
\boxed{
\text{Knowledge Producers}
\longleftrightarrow
\text{Professional Engineers}
}
\]
No single civil engineering society needs to produce every specialist course itself.
Structural engineering, geotechnical engineering, concrete, water resources, coastal and ocean engineering, tunneling, transportation, and construction management already have specialist communities with deep knowledge.
A consortium of professional societies could form a knowledge ecosystem in which specialist communities retain their depth while engineers gain access to credible knowledge across disciplinary boundaries.
That is a more valuable role than simply adding another provider to a regulated training market.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: Engineers at different career stages should not learn the same things
text:
Engineers at different career stages should not learn the same things
Professional development should also change with responsibility.
An engineer entering practice may need safety, ethics, regulations, contracts, and the practical organization of engineering work that university education cannot fully reproduce.
Later, technical specialization becomes more important.
At senior levels, the challenge changes again. The central skill is no longer the speed with which one calculation can be performed. Senior engineers must integrate results from several disciplines, reason under incomplete information, manage risk, make decisions, and accept responsibility for those decisions.
A career-long learning trajectory may therefore look more like
\[
\text{Fundamentals}
\rightarrow
\text{Professional Practice}
\rightarrow
\text{Specialization}
\rightarrow
\text{Integration and Judgment}
\rightarrow
\text{Leadership}.
\]
As responsibility increases, the ability to identify what one needs to learn becomes increasingly important.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: University education and CPD are the same problem at different times
text:
University education and CPD are the same problem at different times
University civil engineering education and continuing professional development are usually administered as separate systems.
Educationally, however, they are different stages of the same question:
What kind of civil engineer are we trying to develop?
Universities should provide deep and durable fundamentals, a structured view of the wider infrastructure system, and enough technical depth for students to begin solving genuine engineering problems.
Practice then develops the ability to work with real constraints, uncertainty, institutions, people, and consequences.
CPD keeps professional knowledge current and expands it as technology and societal needs change.
At senior levels, integration, judgment, ethics, risk, and leadership become increasingly important.
All of this is civil engineering education.
It is therefore too narrow to define civil engineering education only as a university curriculum.
It is equally narrow to define continuing education only as mandatory training.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
section: Start with the engineer we want to develop
text:
Start with the engineer we want to develop
Adding an AI course to a mandatory training program will not solve this problem. Neither will adding more BIM hours or moving more lectures online.
Those may be useful changes, but they come later.
First, we need a clear idea of the engineer we are trying to develop.
A civil engineer is not merely someone who executes a predetermined construction task. A civil engineer understands natural and human systems; plans, analyzes, designs, constructs, operates, and maintains infrastructure; and adapts engineering practice as technology, environmental conditions, and societal needs change.
If civil engineering is reduced to construction engineering, its educational system will inherit the same narrow boundary.
If engineers are treated primarily as people whose training hours must be administratively verified, the training market may function efficiently without guaranteeing continuing professional growth.
The principle I took away from the February discussion is therefore simple:

Do not design the education system before deciding what kind of engineer the system is meant to develop.

Universities should teach durable principles deeply.
Practice should connect those principles to real engineering problems.
CPD should enable engineers to keep updating their professional map throughout their careers.
When these stages are connected, continuing education becomes more than a compliance requirement.
It becomes infrastructure for the lifelong development of civil engineers.

title: What Should a Civil Engineer Learn over a Career?
text:

ABET, Criteria for Accrediting Engineering Programs, 2025–2026
Institution of Civil Engineers, Continuing Professional Development
Engineers Australia, CPD Requirements
ASCE Policy Statement 425, Continuing Professional Development for Licensure

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
text:
English | 한글
A waste material can be chemically reactive.
That sounds useful.
But the same reactivity can also destroy concrete.
This apparent contradiction has followed one line of our research for more than two decades.
It began around 2000 with a deceptively simple question about waste glass:
At that time, the problem was alkali-silica reaction (ASR). Waste glass used as aggregate could react with the alkaline pore solution of concrete, produce expansive reaction products, and cause cracking.
But the experiments revealed something much more interesting than simply
\[
\text{glass}
\rightarrow
\text{ASR}
\rightarrow
\text{damage}.
\]
Particle size changed the outcome.
Making glass particles smaller initially increased the damaging expansion.
Then, below a certain size, the trend reversed.
Eventually the glass became sufficiently fine that the harmful macroscopic expansion disappeared.
That observation led Zdeněk P. Bažant, Christian Meyer, and me to examine the problem using fracture mechanics.
More than two decades later, the same basic mechanics unexpectedly reappeared in our research on basic oxygen furnace (BOF) slag.
The chemistry was different.
The waste material was different.
But the central mechanics question was remarkably similar:
The answer, in both cases, depends strongly on particle size.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: The story began with a crack
text:
The story began with a crack
Consider a reactive particle embedded in a cementitious matrix.
If a chemical reaction produces an expansive product around that particle, the reaction creates pressure against the surrounding material.
The important sequence is therefore
\[
\text{chemical reaction}
\rightarrow
\text{expansion}
\rightarrow
\text{pressure}
\rightarrow
\text{stress}
\rightarrow
\text{cracking}.
\]
Chemistry initiates the process.
But mechanics determines whether the surrounding concrete actually cracks.



The original fracture-mechanics picture of a reactive glass particle. ASR product forms around the particle and generates pressure against the surrounding cement matrix. The engineering problem is therefore not chemical reaction alone, but whether that reaction can drive a crack.


In our 2000 study, the glass particle was idealized as an expanding inclusion surrounded by mortar.
Alkali-silica reaction occurred near the glass surface, and the resulting expansive gel generated pressure against the surrounding cementitious matrix.
Existing flaws around the particle could then grow into cracks.
This immediately suggests a fracture-mechanics question.
It is not enough to ask:

How much reaction product is generated?

We must also ask:

Is the resulting pressure capable of driving a crack?

That distinction became essential for understanding the particle-size effect.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
text:
Why should particle size matter?
One might initially expect a simple relationship.
Smaller particles have larger surface area per unit mass.
More surface area should promote reaction.
Therefore,
\[
\text{smaller particles}
\rightarrow
\text{more reaction}
\rightarrow
\text{more expansion}.
\]
But that was not what the experiments showed.
The relationship between particle size and ASR damage was non-monotonic.
As the glass particles became smaller, expansion initially increased.
A maximum occurred at an intermediate particle size—the so-called pessimum size.
When the particles became still smaller, expansion decreased again.
In the accelerated tests considered in the 2000 study, the pessimum size was around the millimeter scale, while adverse expansion was no longer detectable when the glass particles became sufficiently fine.



The counterintuitive particle-size effect that motivated the fracture-mechanics model. Reducing glass-particle size initially increases ASR damage, but below a pessimum size the trend reverses. A more reactive particle does not necessarily produce more structural damage.


This is the first important clue.

Chemical reactivity and structural damage are not the same thing.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
text:
Two competing size effects
Why can smaller particles eventually become less damaging even though they may react more readily?
Because two mechanisms compete.
The first is chemical.
Reducing particle size increases the available reactive surface.
Schematically,
\[
d\downarrow
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\frac{A}{V}\uparrow
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\text{reaction potential}\uparrow.
\]
This tends to increase reaction.
But there is another mechanism.
A crack must obtain enough energy from the expanding particle to propagate through the surrounding matrix.
As the characteristic particle size decreases, the spatial scale over which the expansive reaction acts also decreases.
The ability of an individual particle to generate and drive a macroscopic crack therefore changes.
In fracture-mechanics terms, the question becomes whether the energy available from expansion is sufficient to overcome the resistance associated with crack growth.
So particle size affects both
\[
\boxed{
\text{reaction}
}
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\text{fracture}.
}
\]
These two effects do not scale in the same way.
That is why a pessimum size can exist.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: More reaction does not necessarily mean more damage
text:
More reaction does not necessarily mean more damage
This was the conceptual result that stayed with me.
Suppose we reduce the size of a reactive particle.
Its chemistry may become more active because more surface is exposed.
But the reaction also becomes distributed over a much larger number of smaller particles.
Instead of a few strong localized expansion sources, we may obtain many smaller reaction sites.
The mechanical picture changes from something like
\[
\boxed{\text{large particle}}
\rightarrow
\text{localized expansion}
\rightarrow
\text{high local crack-driving action}
\]
toward
\[
\boxed{\text{many fine particles}}
\rightarrow
\text{distributed reaction}
\rightarrow
\text{distributed deformation}.
\]
The chemistry has not disappeared.
What has changed is how the chemical reaction enters the mechanics of the material.
That distinction eventually changed the engineering question completely.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: What if glass becomes sufficiently fine?
text:
What if glass becomes sufficiently fine?
Once glass particles become very fine, perhaps we should stop thinking of them as aggregate.
They begin to behave more like a powder.
And that suggests a different role.
Glass contains large amounts of silica, much of it in an amorphous state.
Finely divided glass can therefore participate in pozzolanic reactions.
The engineering question then changes from

How can we stop waste glass from damaging concrete?

to

Can we use its reactivity beneficially?

This is a profound reversal.
The same basic material moves from
\[
\text{potentially harmful reactive aggregate}
\]
to
\[
\text{potentially useful supplementary cementitious material}.
\]
The boundary between the two is strongly influenced by particle size.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: From waste glass aggregate to waste glass powder
text:
From waste glass aggregate to waste glass powder
Our later research returned repeatedly to this idea using different sources of waste glass.
One example was waste glass sludge produced during glass manufacturing.
Fine glass dust generated during cutting and polishing is washed away with water. During wastewater treatment, precipitation additives are used to help separate the glass particles, producing a sludge cake.
After drying and grinding, that industrial waste becomes a fine powder.



Waste glass sludge after drying and grinding, together with its particle-size distribution. Once waste glass is reduced from aggregate-scale particles to fine powder, the engineering question changes from how to prevent ASR damage to how to exploit its pozzolanic reactivity.


Our 2016 study compared waste glass sludge produced with precipitation additives with corresponding glass sludge prepared without those additives.
An unexpected result emerged.
The sludge containing the precipitation additives showed greater pozzolanic potential.
The waste-treatment process had not merely separated the glass.
It had altered the subsequent behavior of the material.
In particular, caustic soda used during wastewater treatment is itself associated with alkaline activation.
So an industrial processing history that might initially appear irrelevant to concrete performance became part of the material’s reactivity.
This is another useful lesson in waste utilization:

A waste material is defined not only by what it is chemically, but also by what has happened to it before we receive it.

The 2016 study explicitly situated this work within the earlier particle-size research: fineness had become one of the key parameters governing whether waste glass could be used beneficially as a concrete admixture.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
text:
Then came LCD glass
The research subsequently moved to another industrial glass waste: liquid-crystal-display glass.
LCD glass was particularly interesting because its composition differs from ordinary soda-lime container glass.
It contains substantial amorphous silica and alumina while having very low alkali content.
That combination made it promising as a supplementary cementitious material.
The research question was no longer simply

Is fine glass safe?

It became

What useful properties can fine waste glass give to concrete?

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: From avoiding ASR to improving durability
text:
From avoiding ASR to improving durability
In concrete pavement applications, LCD glass powder was investigated as a partial cement replacement.
The material satisfied the relevant chemical and physical requirements considered for a Class F pozzolanic admixture.
More importantly, incorporating LCD glass powder improved resistance to two important deterioration mechanisms:

alkali-silica reaction,
chloride penetration.

Its later-age strength development and resistance to freezing and thawing were also comparable to those of the fly-ash concrete examined in the study.
This is an interesting point in the research history.
The original 2000 problem was:
\[
\boxed{\text{glass causes ASR}}
\]
Yet sufficiently fine and appropriately composed waste glass could later be used to help produce concrete with greater resistance to ASR.
That is not a contradiction.
It is a consequence of changing the scale and role of the material.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: The powder eventually became part of the mechanics
text:
The powder eventually became part of the mechanics
The research then moved beyond conventional concrete durability.
LCD glass powder was incorporated into ultra-high-performance fiber-reinforced concrete.
Here the important question was not simply whether glass could replace another powder.
The matrix controls how steel fibers interact with the surrounding cementitious material.
That means changing the powder can eventually change
\[
\text{matrix}
\rightarrow
\text{fiber-matrix interface}
\rightarrow
\text{fiber pullout}
\rightarrow
\text{tensile behavior}.
\]
In one study, replacing quartz powder with LCD glass powder up to an appropriate level enhanced the matrix through pozzolanic reaction despite changes in packing density.
At 50% replacement of quartz powder, the reported fiber-pullout energy was 142% higher than that of the reference UHPC matrix.
The corresponding UHPFRC showed increases of 150% in tensile strain capacity and 174% in energy absorption relative to the reference material.
These numbers belong to that particular mixture and curing system and should not be treated as general factors.
But their mechanical meaning is important.
The waste powder had progressed from something whose cracking effect needed to be controlled to something capable of modifying the tensile response of a high-performance composite.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: Glass also became a chemical component of new binders
text:
Glass also became a chemical component of new binders
The next step moved still further away from the original aggregate problem.
LCD glass powder was combined with blast-furnace slag in alkali-activated materials.
Now the glass was not simply replacing aggregate or conventional filler.
It was participating directly in binder chemistry.
The 2023 study found that replacing slag with LCD glass powder up to 50% could be achieved without strength loss under the investigated conditions, while 25% LCD glass powder improved pore structure and precursor reactivity.
But excessive LCD glass powder—more than 50% in that system—reduced the pore-solution pH, reduced precursor reactivity, and caused significant strength loss.
Again we encounter the same engineering principle:
\[
\boxed{
\text{more of a beneficial mechanism}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{better performance indefinitely}.
}
\]
There is usually an optimum governed by competing mechanisms.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: Then a different waste material brought us back to 2000
text:
Then a different waste material brought us back to 2000
More recently, we began investigating basic oxygen furnace slag.
BOF slag is produced during steelmaking.
At first sight, this seems to be a very different problem from waste glass.
Glass-related expansion is associated with alkali-silica reaction.
The principal volume-instability concern considered in our BOF study is associated with free CaO.
Free CaO hydrates according to
\[
\mathrm{CaO}+\mathrm{H_2O}
\rightarrow
\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}.
\]
The reaction produces substantial volume expansion.
If that expansion occurs locally inside a cementitious matrix, stresses develop around the reacting slag particle.
And suddenly the mechanics looks familiar.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
text:
Different chemistry, same mechanics
For waste glass:
\[
\text{ASR}
\rightarrow
\text{expansive reaction product}
\rightarrow
\text{local pressure}
\rightarrow
\text{cracking}.
\]
For BOF slag:
\[
\text{free-CaO hydration}
\rightarrow
\text{volume increase}
\rightarrow
\text{local expansive stress}
\rightarrow
\text{cracking}.
\]
The chemical reactions are different.
But from the viewpoint of the surrounding cementitious matrix, both problems contain an expanding inclusion.
That takes us back to the question we had asked more than two decades earlier:

How does the size of the reactive particle control whether expansion becomes cracking?

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: Coarse BOF slag localizes the expansion
text:
Coarse BOF slag localizes the expansion
Our 2026 study classified BOF slag into nine particle-size fractions ranging from below 45 \(\mu\)m to several millimeters and examined their expansion behavior at different incorporation ratios.
The results were strongly size dependent.
Coarse particles produced localized hydration and concentrated expansive stresses.
Cracks and pop-outs developed around those particles.
Finer particles behaved differently.
The hydration reactions became more spatially distributed, and macroscopic cracking was suppressed.



Particle-size-dependent expansion and cracking of BOF slag. Although the chemistry differs from ASR in waste glass, the mechanics is familiar: a coarse reactive particle localizes expansion and generates concentrated stresses, whereas sufficiently fine particles distribute the reaction and suppress macroscopic cracking.


The experimental observations were particularly revealing.
For the conditions investigated, all BOF slag fractions of 600 \(\mu\)m and above eventually fractured.
The 600 \(\mu\)m fraction exhibited especially severe deterioration, showing that the relationship between particle size and damage was again not simply monotonic.
At a 10% incorporation ratio, no visible cracking or pop-outs were observed for particles finer than approximately 300 \(\mu\)m.
At the higher 20% incorporation ratio, a finer particle size was needed to maintain comparable stability.
So once again,
\[
\boxed{
\text{particle size governs whether local chemical expansion becomes structural damage}.
}
\]

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: Why do fine particles behave differently?
text:
Why do fine particles behave differently?
Imagine the same amount of reactive material divided into different particle sizes.
With coarse particles, the expansive reaction is concentrated at relatively few locations.
Each particle acts as a larger local expansion source.
Schematically,
\[
\text{few coarse particles}
\rightarrow
\text{localized reaction}
\rightarrow
\text{concentrated stress}
\rightarrow
\text{crack}.
\]
When the same material is divided into many finer particles,
\[
\text{many fine particles}
\rightarrow
\text{distributed reaction}
\rightarrow
\text{distributed stress}
\rightarrow
\text{reduced macroscopic damage}.
\]
This is not merely a chemical explanation.
It is a mechanical length-scale argument.
The characteristic size of the expanding region matters relative to the surrounding material’s ability to accommodate deformation and resist fracture.
That is why the conceptual connection to the earlier waste-glass research is so strong.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: But should we simply grind everything as finely as possible?
text:
But should we simply grind everything as finely as possible?
This is where the BOF-slag problem adds another dimension to the original glass story.
Suppose smaller particles suppress expansion.
Then the simplest recommendation might seem obvious:

Grind the slag as finely as possible.

But grinding requires energy.
And BOF slag is particularly difficult to grind because of its hardness and high iron content.
So particle-size reduction has both a benefit and a cost.
The real engineering problem is therefore not
\[
\min d.
\]
It is something closer to
\[
\boxed{
\text{find }d
\text{ that is sufficiently small for stability,
but not unnecessarily small}.
}
\]

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: There is a point where more grinding gives little benefit
text:
There is a point where more grinding gives little benefit
The BOF study provides a particularly useful comparison.
As particle size decreased, the 28-day compressive strength generally improved, with a pronounced improvement in the range below approximately 300 \(\mu\)m.
That range also corresponded to the expansion-stable region identified for the lower incorporation ratio.
But grinding energy rises rapidly as the target particle size becomes smaller.
Using Bond’s law, the relative grinding-energy demand can be represented as
\[
W
\propto
\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_p}}
-
\frac{1}{\sqrt{d_f}},
\]
where \(d_f\) is the feed size and \(d_p\) is the desired product size.



Particle size is not only a materials variable but also an engineering design variable. Finer BOF slag improves expansion stability and strength, but the grinding-energy demand rises rapidly. The practical objective is therefore not the smallest possible particle, but the coarsest particle that safely changes the damage mechanism.


For the assumptions used in the study, reducing the BOF slag to approximately
\[
300~\mu\mathrm{m}
\]
required only about 15% of the estimated grinding energy required to reach 45 \(\mu\)m.
In other words, pushing the material all the way into the ultrafine range requires a disproportionately large additional energy input.
If the mechanical problem has already been controlled, that additional grinding may provide little engineering value.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: The threshold depends on how much slag we use
text:
The threshold depends on how much slag we use
There is an important qualification.
There is no universal particle size below which BOF slag automatically becomes safe.
Particle size interacts with incorporation ratio.
At a higher slag content, more reactive particles are present simultaneously and less surrounding pore space is available to accommodate the reaction products.
Consequently, the same particle size can become more damaging when more BOF slag is incorporated.
Under the conditions investigated in the 2026 study, a particle size below approximately
\[
300~\mu\mathrm{m}
\]
was adequate at an incorporation ratio of about 10%, whereas a ratio approaching 20% required finer grinding, around
\[
75~\mu\mathrm{m}.
\]
These values are not universal design limits.
They depend on mixture design, slag characteristics, free-CaO content, and exposure conditions.
But they demonstrate something much more general:

Particle size should be designed together with the amount of reactive material.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
text:
A 25-year research question
Looking back, what interests me most is not that the research began with waste glass and eventually arrived at BOF slag.
It is that the same question kept returning in different forms.
Around 2000, the question was:

Why does waste-glass particle size produce a pessimum ASR response?

Fracture mechanics showed that reaction alone could not explain the observation.
Later, the question became:

Can sufficiently fine waste glass be used rather than merely tolerated?

The answer led toward waste-glass sludge, LCD glass powder, durability, UHPC, and alkali-activated binders.
Then BOF slag brought the problem back to expansive particles:

How small must a reactive slag particle become before its expansion no longer produces damaging cracks?

And finally:

How much grinding is actually necessary to achieve that change?

The research path can therefore be summarized as
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
\text{reactive particle}
&\rightarrow
\text{fracture mechanics}
\\
&\rightarrow
\text{particle-size effect}
\\
&\rightarrow
\text{fine reactive powder}
\\
&\rightarrow
\text{useful cementitious material}
\\
&\rightarrow
\text{particle-size design}.
\end{aligned}
}
\]

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: The real variable is not simply particle size
text:
The real variable is not simply particle size
Particle size is the variable we can measure and control.
But mechanically, something deeper is happening.
By changing particle size, we change the spatial distribution of chemical reaction.
That changes the spatial distribution of expansion.
That changes the stress field.
And that changes the ability of cracks to initiate and propagate.
So the deeper chain is
\[
\boxed{
\text{particle size}
\rightarrow
\text{reaction localization}
\rightarrow
\text{expansion localization}
\rightarrow
\text{stress localization}
\rightarrow
\text{fracture}.
}
\]
This is why particle-size control can transform a material from damaging to useful.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: Waste utilization should be a mechanics problem too
text:
Waste utilization should be a mechanics problem too
Waste recycling in concrete is often discussed primarily in terms of

chemical composition,
replacement ratio,
compressive strength,
carbon reduction,
and disposal volume.

All of these are important.
But reactive industrial wastes also pose a mechanics problem.
A material may contain a chemically unstable phase.
That does not automatically mean it cannot be used.
The relevant engineering questions are:

How fast does it react?
How much does it expand?
Over what spatial scale does the reaction occur?
What stress field does that expansion generate?
Can the surrounding matrix accommodate it?
Can the reaction drive a crack?
What processing is required to move the system into a stable regime?

This is where materials chemistry and fracture mechanics meet.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
section: Why the finest powder is not necessarily the best powder
text:
Why the finest powder is not necessarily the best powder
There is a tendency in supplementary cementitious-material research to associate greater fineness with better performance.
Often that is partly true.
Finer particles provide greater surface area and can improve packing or accelerate reaction.
But engineering optimization should not ask
\[
\text{How fine can we grind it?}
\]
It should ask
\[
\boxed{
\text{How fine does it need to be?}
}
\]
Once particle size is below the threshold required to suppress the damaging mechanism, additional grinding must justify its additional energy and cost.
This distinction becomes particularly important when the objective of waste utilization is sustainability.
Using an industrial by-product is not automatically sustainable if making it usable requires unnecessary processing energy.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
text:
Limitations
The numerical thresholds discussed here should not be transferred directly from one waste material or mixture to another.
The 2000 waste-glass results concerned alkali-silica reaction under specific accelerated experimental conditions and a particular glass-concrete system.
The later waste-glass studies examined different sources of glass, processing histories, particle sizes, binder systems, and curing conditions.
The BOF-slag study used a particular slag source and evaluated incorporation ratios of 10% and 20% under specified accelerated expansion conditions.
Its particle-size thresholds therefore apply to the investigated system rather than defining universal limits for BOF slag.
Likewise, the grinding-energy comparison was based on an idealized Bond-law estimate rather than a complete industrial life-cycle or economic analysis.
The broader conclusion is not a universal number such as
\[
300~\mu\mathrm{m}.
\]
It is the mechanics behind that number.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
text:
Engineering takeaway
A reactive waste particle can be harmful when its reaction is sufficiently localized to generate a crack.
The same material, when sufficiently fine, can distribute that reaction over a smaller spatial scale and may become a useful component of a cementitious system.
That is why the transition
\[
\text{waste aggregate}
\rightarrow
\text{reactive powder}
\]
can completely change engineering performance.
The lesson from waste glass eventually became a useful way to think about BOF slag.
And the practical conclusion is deliberately not

Grind reactive waste as finely as possible.

It is:

Grind it as finely as necessary to change the mechanics from localized damage to distributed reaction.

For BOF slag, that becomes an even simpler engineering rule:

Do not grind BOF slag as finely as possible. Grind it as finely as necessary.

title: Why Can a Harmful Waste Particle Become a Useful Concrete Material?
