title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
text:
English | 한글
For me, LaTeX is not simply a typesetting program.
It is the infrastructure of research writing.
Over many years of writing technical papers, equations, reports, lectures, and presentations, I gradually developed a system in which the scientific content is separated from the formatting required by a particular journal or document type.
The basic idea is simple:
This distinction has become increasingly important to me because individual papers come and go, journals have different formats, and presentation styles continue to change. The underlying research material, however, should remain reusable.
My system therefore has several persistent components:
The same technical material can later be converted into a publisher’s journal format, reused in another paper, or reorganized into a Beamer presentation.
The important point is not any individual file.
It is the system connecting them.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
section: Why I do not begin with a journal template
text:
Why I do not begin with a journal template
When starting a research paper, I normally do not begin by adapting my thinking to the formatting rules of the target journal.
Instead, I begin from my own template.tex.
This gives me a familiar and stable writing environment. The manuscript develops around the research question, equations, figures, references, results, and discussion rather than around the visual style of a publisher.
This creates a useful separation:
scientific writing
        ≠
journal formatting
The scientific paper should first become correct, coherent, and complete as a technical document.
Only later do I change the styling for the journal of choice.
That may involve changing:

the document class,
front matter,
title and author formatting,
section styles,
bibliography style,
figure placement rules,
table formatting,
supplementary-material conventions,
or publisher-specific commands.

The research content should not have to be rebuilt simply because the journal changes.
This is one of the main reasons I prefer a personal LaTeX writing environment.

The manuscript changes from paper to paper. The research-writing infrastructure does not.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
text:
Shared packages: zipackage.tex
A technical paper repeatedly needs the same kinds of LaTeX support.
Mathematics, graphics, tables, bibliography handling, algorithms, nomenclature, TikZ, and theorem-like environments are not unique requirements of one manuscript. They recur across many projects.
I therefore collect the packages that I commonly use in a shared file, zipackage.tex.
Representative parts include packages such as:
\usepackage{amsmath}
\usepackage{amssymb}
\usepackage{multirow}
\usepackage{appendix}
\usepackage[noprefix]{nomencl}
\usepackage[comma,numbers,sort&compress]{natbib}

\usepackage{tikz}
\usepackage{pgfplots}

\usepackage{algorithmicx}
\usepackage{algpseudocode}
The file has grown over time to support the kinds of technical documents I actually write.
It includes recurring support for such things as:

mathematical notation,
symbols,
graphics and PDF graphics,
hyperlinks,
tables,
appendices,
nomenclature,
bibliography management,
TikZ drawings,
PGFPlots,
theorem-like constructs,
algorithms,
and other technical-writing needs.

The main advantage is not that I can load many packages at once.
The real advantage is that repeated technical configuration has one authoritative location.
If a recurring setting has to be corrected or improved, I can change it in the common infrastructure rather than repair the same issue separately in many manuscripts.
This is similar to software development: repeated functionality should not be copied unnecessarily into every project.
At the same time, I would not recommend that another researcher simply copy a large package file and load everything.
A useful shared package file should grow gradually from real writing needs.
Mine reflects years of mechanics and engineering writing.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
text:
Shared commands: zicommand.tex
The second common file, zicommand.tex, is even more personal.
At first glance, custom commands may look like typing shortcuts.
For example:
\newcommand{\sig}{\sigma}
\newcommand{\eps}{\epsilon}
\newcommand{\veps}{\varepsilon}
\newcommand{\del}{\delta}
\newcommand{\Del}{\Delta}
\newcommand{\la}{\lambda}
\newcommand{\om}{\omega}
But after many years, the command set becomes much more than a collection of abbreviations.
It becomes a personal technical vocabulary.
My command file contains recurring notation and formatting associated with engineering mechanics, including commands for:

tensors,
bold symbols,
jump notation,
units,
cross-references,
table formatting,
TikZ dimensioning,
hypotheses and theorem-like constructs,
revision marking,
and technical notation accumulated through repeated research projects.

For example, revision commands can be defined once:
\newcommand{\chgI}[1]{{\color{DarkRed}{#1}}}
\newcommand{\chgII}[1]{{\color{DarkBlue}{#1}}}
Then the revision mechanism can be used consistently throughout a manuscript.
This suggests a deeper principle:

Commands should represent concepts, not merely save keystrokes.

The relationship is
physical or writing concept
        ↓
personal LaTeX command
        ↓
printed notation
This helps maintain consistency.
If I decide to change how a quantity is represented, I can often change the command definition rather than manually searching for every occurrence in a long manuscript.
For technical writing, that is particularly valuable because notation is part of the argument. A symbol should not silently change meaning or appearance halfway through a paper.
This connects directly to one part of my broader CCC writing principle: Consistency.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
text:
One master bibliography: reference.bib
I also maintain one large BibTeX database rather than starting a new bibliography from zero for each paper.
The file, reference.bib, has accumulated over many years.
It contains ordinary bibliographic information, but over time it has become much more than a mechanism for producing a reference list.
The database includes such information as:

authors,
titles,
journals,
years,
volumes and pages,
DOI and URL information where available,
journal abbreviations,
subject keywords,
and in some entries additional notes or abstracts.

I also use journal @STRING definitions for recurring abbreviations such as
CMAME
IJNME
IJSS
JEM
JSE
OE
...
and subject codes accumulated around my research areas, for example:
FR    fracture mechanics
PL    plasticity
XF    XFEM
FS    floating structures / hydromechanics
FAT   fatigue
HE    hydroelasticity
...
As the database grows, it becomes a record of the literature that has accompanied my research career.
For this reason, I no longer regard reference.bib simply as a bibliography generator.

It is a personal research-memory database.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
section: One identifier for the citation, metadata, and PDF
text:
One identifier for the citation, metadata, and PDF
The most important part of my reference system is the relationship between BibTeX and the original PDF files.
I keep the source papers themselves in a large reference archive.
The rule is simple:

The PDF filename is identical to the BibTeX key.

Suppose I assign a paper the key
AlSNah18
I cite it in LaTeX as
\cite{AlSNah18}
The corresponding entry in reference.bib begins with
@article{AlSNah18,
  ...
}
and the original source paper is stored as
AlSNah18.pdf
Therefore the same identifier connects three different things:
\cite{AlSNah18}
        ↕
@article{AlSNah18,...}
        ↕
AlSNah18.pdf
or, more generally,
citation
   ↕
bibliographic metadata
   ↕
original source document
This is one of the most useful habits I have developed.






Figure 1: My research-paper archive. Each PDF filename is the BibTeX key used in my master bibliography and LaTeX manuscripts. A citation key therefore points not only to bibliographic metadata but also directly to the original source document.



Figure Figure 1 shows part of the actual archive.
The filenames are not arbitrary descriptions of the papers. They are the same identifiers used in BibTeX.
This means that when I encounter a citation key in an old manuscript, I can immediately find the corresponding source PDF.
The key is therefore not only a citation label.
It is the permanent identity of the reference within my research system.

Give every reference one identifier, and use that same identifier everywhere.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
section: How I add a new reference
text:
How I add a new reference
When I obtain a new paper, I add it to the system through a consistent sequence.
1. Obtain the paper
2. Verify or create the BibTeX metadata
3. Assign the BibTeX key
4. Rename the PDF using exactly the same key
5. Store the PDF in the reference archive
6. Cite the paper using that same key
For example:
BibTeX key      AlSNah18
BibTeX record   @article{AlSNah18,...}
PDF file        AlSNah18.pdf
LaTeX citation  \cite{AlSNah18}
Nothing has to be translated from one naming system into another.
That becomes increasingly important after the archive contains hundreds or thousands of papers.
A descriptive filename may be meaningful when a paper is first downloaded, but years later it may be difficult to remember exactly how it was named.
A permanent citation key solves that problem.
The manuscript itself tells me how to retrieve the original paper.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
section: How I start a new manuscript
text:
How I start a new manuscript
With the persistent infrastructure already established, beginning a new research paper becomes systematic.
My workflow is approximately:
1. Start from template.tex
2. Define the root and common paths
3. Load zipackage.tex
4. Load zicommand.tex
5. Set the local figure directory
6. Write the paper-specific manuscript
7. Store figures with the manuscript
8. Cite literature using keys from reference.bib
9. Retrieve source PDFs using those same keys
10. Compile and revise in the stable environment
11. Adapt the finished manuscript to the target journal template
The important distinction is between what belongs to a particular paper and what belongs to my research-writing infrastructure.
Paper-specific material includes:
manuscript
figures
tables
calculations
results
journal-specific files
The persistent layer includes:
template.tex
zipackage.tex
zicommand.tex
reference.bib
References/*.pdf
This separation is what makes the workflow reusable.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
text:
The journal template comes later
Eventually, a manuscript must satisfy the requirements of a specific journal.
At that point I may have to move the scientific content into a publisher’s class file or template.
But by then the main intellectual work has already been done.
The equations exist.
The figures exist.
The references exist.
The notation is consistent.
The argument has been developed.
The conversion is therefore primarily a change in presentation and submission structure rather than a reconstruction of the research paper.
Conceptually:
my stable manuscript
        ↓
scientific content completed
        ↓
target journal selected
        ↓
publisher class/template applied
        ↓
final submission
This way of working is especially useful when the target journal changes during the publication process.
The research should not be locked into the visual assumptions of the first journal considered.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
section: LaTeX content is reusable beyond papers
text:
LaTeX content is reusable beyond papers
Another important benefit of this system is that LaTeX content is not limited to a single journal manuscript.
A research project produces many reusable objects:

equations,
symbols,
derivations,
figures,
TikZ drawings,
tables,
references,
explanations,
and technical terminology.

Because these objects are stored as structured source material, they can be reorganized for other purposes.
One of the clearest examples is Beamer.
Material developed for a paper can later be reused in a presentation:
research idea
      ↓
LaTeX equations + figures + references
      ↓
journal manuscript
      │
      ├──→ another journal format
      │
      ├──→ conference paper
      │
      ├──→ Beamer presentation
      │
      ├──→ lecture material
      │
      └──→ later technical writing
The point is not simply that Beamer can make presentation slides.
The more important point is that the same technical source can serve more than one communication purpose.
An equation written carefully for a paper does not need to be reconstructed in PowerPoint.
A TikZ figure can often be reused.
Technical notation remains the same.
Bibliographic keys remain the same.
The research content can therefore move from one document form to another with much less duplication.
This is where LaTeX becomes more than a typesetting tool.
It becomes a reusable representation of technical knowledge.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
section: Why the system becomes more valuable with time
text:
Why the system becomes more valuable with time
The value of this approach is modest when writing the first paper.
It becomes much larger after many papers.
A shared command file may initially save only a few keystrokes.
After years of work, it encodes a substantial part of one’s technical notation.
A BibTeX database may initially contain a few dozen references.
After decades, it becomes a map of the literature encountered throughout a research career.
A PDF naming rule may initially look unnecessarily strict.
After thousands of citations, it provides a direct connection between old manuscripts and their original sources.
This leads to an important difference between ordinary document organization and research infrastructure.
individual papers are temporary
research infrastructure is persistent
Each new project uses the infrastructure, but it also contributes to it.
New commands may be added.
New packages may become necessary.
New references enter the bibliography and PDF archive.
New figures and explanations may later become teaching material.
The system therefore grows with the research itself.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
section: A foundation for a future research knowledge system
text:
A foundation for a future research knowledge system
There is another consequence that has become increasingly interesting with the development of AI-assisted research tools.
The citation key already connects several forms of information:
BibTeX metadata
      +
source PDF
      +
topic keywords
      +
manuscript citations
That structure could support future tools for:

semantic literature search,
citation verification,
topic clustering,
literature maps,
retrieval-augmented generation,
source-grounded AI writing,
and reconstruction of one’s own research history.

I do not yet regard this as the primary reason for maintaining the system.
The system was developed to solve a much more basic problem: how to write technical research efficiently and consistently over a long period.
But a well-structured research archive has consequences that extend beyond LaTeX itself.
Once references, source documents, notation, and manuscripts already have persistent identities and relationships, they are much easier to connect to new computational tools.

title: How I Built a Reusable LaTeX System for Research Writing
text:
The main principle
Looking back, the most important feature of my LaTeX workflow is not any package, command, template, or bibliography style.
It is the decision to treat research writing as a persistent system rather than a sequence of isolated documents.
My papers change.
My research topics evolve.
Journal formats change.
Presentation formats change.
But the underlying infrastructure continues to accumulate value.
That is why I would summarize the entire workflow in one principle:

Do not organize research around individual documents. Build a persistent writing system from which individual documents are produced.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: What my existing template is doing

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
text:
Start from the data hierarchy
Before writing any LaTeX, I find it useful to sketch the logical hierarchy of the table.
Suppose the data have this form:
Test type
├── Biaxial
│   ├── B3
│   ├── B6
│   └── B12
└── Uniaxial
    ├── U3
    ├── U6
    └── U12
The LaTeX table should preserve that hierarchy.
That immediately suggests:
\multicolumn{3}{c}{Biaxial test}
and
\multicolumn{3}{c}{Uniaxial test}
followed by a second header row containing the individual test labels.
This is more than formatting.
The table header is carrying engineering information.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
text:
\multicolumn: one heading over several columns
The first command every technical LaTeX user should understand is \multicolumn.
Its form is
\multicolumn{number of columns}{alignment}{content}
For example,
\multicolumn{3}{c}{Biaxial test}
means that one cell occupies three columns.
A grouped engineering table can therefore be written as
\begin{tabular}{c c c c c c c}
\hline
\multirow{2}{*}{No.} &
\multicolumn{3}{c}{Biaxial test} &
\multicolumn{3}{c}{Uniaxial test} \\
\cline{2-7}
& B3 & B6 & B12 & U3 & U6 & U12 \\
\hline
...
\end{tabular}
The first row tells the reader what the large groups mean.
The second row resolves each group into individual variables.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
text:
\multirow: one label for several rows
Engineering tables often contain another hierarchy.
For example:
Stiffness
  specimen 1
  specimen 2
  specimen 3
  average
Writing stiffness four times would obscure that these rows form one logical group.
The multirow package solves this:
\multirow{4}{*}{Stiffness}
  & specimen 1 & ... \\
  & specimen 2 & ... \\
  & specimen 3 & ... \\
  & average    & ... \\
This is especially useful for:

material properties,
loading conditions,
specimen groups,
damage states,
analysis methods,
and parameter studies.

I would regard multirow as an almost essential package for engineering tables.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
text:
Partial horizontal lines with \cline
Once rows or columns are grouped, a full-width \hline is often too strong.
The existing template uses commands such as
\cline{5-8}
and
\cline{2-7}
A \cline{5-8} rule begins at column 5 and ends at column 8.
That lets us visually separate subheadings without breaking the larger grouping.
This works, but there is now a better option for many publication-quality tables: booktabs.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
text:
Why I recommend booktabs
Traditional LaTeX tables often look like this:
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|}
\hline
A & B & C \\
\hline
...
\hline
\end{tabular}
There is nothing technically wrong with that.
But dense vertical and horizontal grid lines make a technical table harder to read, especially when it contains many numerical columns.
The booktabs package provides
\toprule
\midrule
\bottomrule
and the partial rule
\cmidrule(lr){2-4}
A grouped header can then be written as
\begin{tabular}{lcccccc}
\toprule
& \multicolumn{3}{c}{Biaxial test}
& \multicolumn{3}{c}{Uniaxial test} \\
\cmidrule(lr){2-4}
\cmidrule(lr){5-7}
No. & B3 & B6 & B12 & U3 & U6 & U12 \\
\midrule
...
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
The result is visually lighter and usually easier to scan.
For journal papers and books, this would now be my default style unless a publisher explicitly requires grid lines.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: One issue in my existing template: \hlinewd
text:
One issue in my existing template: \hlinewd
The template uses commands such as
\hlinewd{1.5pt}
to draw a heavier top or bottom rule.
That command is not defined in the uploaded template itself. The preamble imports my external files zipackage, zicommand, and rgb, so its exact definition must be in one of those files.
That works well inside my own environment, but it has one disadvantage:

the table is not completely portable by itself.

If I send the table to someone who does not have my private command definitions, \hlinewd may fail.
For reusable examples and public templates, I would therefore prefer either standard LaTeX commands or booktabs.
This is an important general principle:

A personal macro is useful when it reduces repeated work. A public example is better when its dependencies are obvious.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: Do not type units as ordinary text
text:
Do not type units as ordinary text
The existing tables include units such as
$[\rm MPa]$
and
$\rm [kg/m^3]$
This works, but I would modernize it.
For scientific and engineering documents, I strongly recommend siunitx.
For example:
\usepackage{siunitx}
Then write
\si{\mega\pascal}
or
\si{\kilogram\per\cubic\metre}
A column heading becomes
Apparent modulus (\si{\mega\pascal})
The major advantage is not merely typography.
It gives one consistent representation of units throughout the entire document.
If I later decide to change spacing or unit style, the document can be changed systematically rather than editing hundreds of tables manually.
That is exactly the reason I like LaTeX in the first place.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: siunitx is even more useful for numbers
text:
siunitx is even more useful for numbers
Consider a column containing
0.36
1.22
24.6
22033
A normal centered c column centers the character strings.
It does not understand that these are numbers.
siunitx provides the S column type:
\begin{tabular}{l S S S}
The values can then be aligned numerically, including decimal markers.
For an engineering table, this is a significant improvement.
Compare:
  1.2
 12.34
  0.056
with numbers aligned at the decimal position.
The second representation is easier to compare quantitatively because the reader’s eye does not have to reconstruct the place value.
This is one of the packages I would recommend most strongly for Zi-SEM technical writing.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
text:
array: define better column types
The standard column types are
l   left
c   center
r   right
Engineering tables often need more control.
The array package lets us define reusable column types.
For example:
\usepackage{array}

\newcolumntype{L}[1]{>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{#1}}
\newcolumntype{C}[1]{>{\centering\arraybackslash}p{#1}}
Then
\begin{tabular}{L{3cm} C{2cm} C{2cm}}
creates fixed-width columns while preserving useful alignment.
This is particularly helpful for tables containing explanations or long engineering terminology rather than only numbers.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: tabularx: let one column absorb the available width
text:
tabularx: let one column absorb the available width
Sometimes a table contains one description column and several compact numerical columns.
For example:
Failure mode | Description | Load | Displacement
The description should use whatever horizontal space remains.
tabularx provides the X column:
\usepackage{tabularx}

\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{l X S S}
The X column expands or contracts automatically to make the table fit \textwidth.
This is much better than repeatedly guessing widths such as p{7.3cm}.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: longtable: when the data are longer than one page
text:
longtable: when the data are longer than one page
The flexural-strength example in my template already contains more than thirty data rows.
For still larger datasets, the ordinary table float cannot break across pages.
That is where longtable is useful:
\usepackage{longtable}
It allows a table to continue over several pages and can repeat the header automatically.
This is useful for:

specimen inventories,
material-property databases,
parameter studies,
design tables,
experimental datasets,
and appendices.

I would not use longtable for a table that comfortably fits on one page. But once a table must genuinely span pages, it is the proper tool.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: threeparttable: notes belong to the table

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: A modernized version of the mix table
text:
A modernized version of the mix table
The original mix-proportion table is structurally good.
I would keep the same hierarchy but modernize the typography.
For example:
\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{multirow}
\usepackage{makecell}
\usepackage{siunitx}

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering
\caption{Mix proportions of the concretes.}
\label{tab:mix}

\begin{tabular}{
  S[table-format=2.0]
  S[table-format=3.0]
  S[table-format=1.0]
  S[table-format=2.1]
  *{4}{S[table-format=4.1]}
  S[table-format=1.0]
  S[table-format=1.0]
}
\toprule
{\multirow{2}{*}{\makecell{w/c\\(\%)}}} &
{\multirow{2}{*}{\makecell{Slump\\(\si{\milli\metre})}}} &
{\multirow{2}{*}{\makecell{Air\\(\%)}}} &
{\multirow{2}{*}{\makecell{s/a\\(\%)}}} &
\multicolumn{4}{c}{Weight} &
{\multirow{2}{*}{SP}} &
{\multirow{2}{*}{AE}} \\
\cmidrule(lr){5-8}
& & & &
{w} & {c} & {s} & {g} & & \\
\midrule
35 & 120 & 5 & 39.5 & 193.9 & 553.9 & 64.0 & 1036.3 & 0 & 0 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
The engineering structure is essentially unchanged.
What has improved is:

fewer heavy grid lines,
clearer grouping,
explicit unit handling,
better multiline headings,
and numerical alignment.

That is the kind of modernization I would make without changing the information itself.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: A practical package set for engineering tables
text:
A practical package set for engineering tables
For most of my technical documents, I would recommend starting with:
\usepackage{booktabs}
\usepackage{multirow}
\usepackage{array}
\usepackage{tabularx}
\usepackage{siunitx}
\usepackage{makecell}
\usepackage{threeparttable}
and adding
\usepackage{longtable}
only when multipage tables are needed.
Their roles are different:



Package
Main purpose




booktabs
high-quality horizontal rules


multirow
cells spanning several rows


array
custom column definitions


tabularx
automatic width management


siunitx
units and numerical alignment


makecell
multiline headings and cells


threeparttable
table notes


longtable
multipage tables



I would regard booktabs, multirow, and siunitx as the three most valuable additions for engineering work.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: Packages I would use only when necessary

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: The table should expose the experiment
text:
The table should expose the experiment
There is a deeper reason I prefer structured tables.
Consider a table with the hierarchy
maximum load
├── specimen 1
├── specimen 2
├── specimen 3
├── average
└── ratio to reference
That organization tells the reader how the result was constructed.
The rows are not independent numbers.
They belong to a measurement process:
\[
\text{individual tests}
\rightarrow
\text{summary statistic}
\rightarrow
\text{engineering comparison}.
\]
A good table makes that logic visible before the reader even studies the numbers.
This is exactly the same principle that applies to equations and figures.
The presentation should expose the mechanics of the argument rather than hide it.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
section: Why this becomes even more useful with AI
text:
Why this becomes even more useful with AI
Tables are another place where AI and LaTeX fit naturally.
If the structure is explicit, I can ask an AI to:

add a new test series,
convert units,
compute and insert summary rows,
reorder groups,
change a table from grid style to booktabs,
align numerical columns with siunitx,
detect inconsistent units,
or convert a CSV dataset into a LaTeX table.

Because the result remains plain text, every change can still be inspected with Git.
This is very different from asking an AI to manipulate a visually formatted table whose underlying structure is hidden inside a binary document.
Again, the key principle is the same:

AI becomes more useful when the document structure is explicit.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
text:
My preferred table workflow
For a new engineering table, I would now use the following reasoning.
First ask:

What is the hierarchy of the data?

Then decide which cells are groups and which are individual measurements.
Use \multicolumn for horizontal grouping and \multirow for vertical grouping.
Use booktabs to separate logical regions rather than drawing a box around every cell.
Use siunitx whenever the table contains physical units or columns of numbers.
Use makecell for compact multiline headings.
Use tabularx when text columns must adapt to the page width.
Use longtable only when the table genuinely extends across pages.
And before adding another package, ask whether the difficulty comes from LaTeX or from the structure of the table itself.
A complicated table often becomes much easier once the engineering hierarchy is made explicit.
That is the real advantage of LaTeX.
It does not merely draw the table.
It lets us describe what the table means.

title: How Should Engineers Build Tables in LaTeX?
text:
Source example
The examples discussed here are taken from my working LaTeX template, which uses tabular, \multicolumn, \multirow, \cline, nested tabular cells, and a custom \hlinewd command in several engineering-table examples. The template also loads my own external package and command files, so some personal macros are intentionally defined outside the template itself.

title: KSCE FIRE DRAGONS: How Tennis Connects Civil Engineers Across Generations
text:
English | 한글
The Korean Society of Civil Engineers (KSCE) Tennis Club began in 2012.
Professor Sanghyun Han of Seoil University served as the first president, and I started as the club secretary. Looking back at the early records, we had 21 members in 2013 and 31 registered members by 2014. The club grew faster than I remember.
From 2012 to 2021, Professor Han and I served as president and secretary, respectively. In 2022, I became president, with Executive Director Jin-I Kwak of Yooshin Engineering serving as secretary. Today, 34 dues-paying members belong to the club.
The number, however, is not what interests me most.
For nearly fifteen years we have met every month, played tournaments, shared meals, and visited other organizations for friendly matches. Somewhere along the way, a more interesting question became clear: What kind of club do we actually want this to be?

title: KSCE FIRE DRAGONS: How Tennis Connects Civil Engineers Across Generations
section: Good players are welcome. Good people matter more.
text:
Good players are welcome. Good people matter more.
Of course this is a tennis club. We like tennis, and when a match begins, people want to win.
But after running the club for many years, I have come to think that playing ability is not the most important ingredient of a good club.
The more important question is who you want to play with again next month.
Our members range from their twenties to their seventies. Some compete at a very high amateur level; others are still learning the game. We include professors, government officials, public-corporation employees, engineers from consulting firms, and engineers from construction companies.
That diversity did not happen entirely by accident. Since becoming president, I have tried to keep the club from becoming dominated by one generation, one level of play, one profession, or one organization.
That does not mean, however, that the overall playing level of KSCE FIRE DRAGONS is that of an ordinary recreational club. We have several national-tournament champions, players of comparable competitive level, and former competitive players among our members. A strong player can visit us and still expect a proper match.
The point is that we did not build the club only around strong players. We wanted experienced players, beginners, younger members, and senior members to enjoy the same club. A high standard of play and diversity in membership are not contradictory. I think a good tennis club can—and should—have both.






Figure 2: Monthly meeting at Korea University in October 2018. Regular monthly tennis became the backbone of the club.



Titles do not help much on a tennis court.
A senior executive may partner with a young engineer. People from a university, a public agency, an engineering company, and a contractor may spend the morning hitting balls at one another across the same net. Nobody gives a professor an easier ball simply because he is a professor.
After several hours of tennis, we sit down for a meal. That is when relationships develop that are difficult to create by exchanging business cards at a formal meeting.
To me, that is one of the club’s greatest values.






Figure 3: Monthly meeting in March 2023. Different generations, organizations, and levels of play share the same court.

title: KSCE FIRE DRAGONS: How Tennis Connects Civil Engineers Across Generations
section: The first Saturday of every month
text:
The first Saturday of every month
The center of the club is not a large annual event. It is the monthly meeting.
Except for January and August, our rule is simple: we meet on the first Saturday morning of each month. We also hold tournaments such as the Club President’s Cup, the KSCE President’s Cup, and the Club Advisor’s Cup.
A club survives through regularity more than spectacle. Members need to know that if they go to the court on the first Saturday morning, familiar faces will be there.
All 34 members cannot attend every time. There are business trips, family events, and all the other things that fill a calendar. Someone may disappear for a few months and then return. We pick up a racket and play again as if we met yesterday.
That is what a club is.






Figure 4: The trophy for the 2024 KSCE President’s Cup tennis tournament.



Since 2024, we have also acquired a new tradition: group warm-up exercises before we play.
Professor Seungjun Ahn of Hongik University is in charge. Curiously, the exercises change every time. He says this is because he has designed a diverse program to warm up the whole body.
Well.
I am not entirely sure every member interprets the variation in quite the same way.
In any case, a monthly meeting now begins with Professor Ahn’s instructions and a group of civil engineers trying to follow them.






Figure 5: Warming up together before tennis. Since 2024, Professor Seungjun Ahn has led the exercises. The routine changes every time. He calls it “variety.”

title: KSCE FIRE DRAGONS: How Tennis Connects Civil Engineers Across Generations
section: Tennis is only half the meeting
text:
Tennis is only half the meeting
The monthly gathering does not end when the tennis ends. In some ways, what comes next may be just as important.






Figure 6: After the 2024 KSCE President’s Cup. Time around the table matters almost as much as time on the court.



Over a meal, conversations move from tennis to universities, companies, civil engineering, families, and life in general. You discover sides of people that are difficult to see during formal professional meetings.
This creates a different kind of professional network. We do not first meet because we need something from one another. We first meet because we enjoy the same sport.
That difference matters.

title: KSCE FIRE DRAGONS: How Tennis Connects Civil Engineers Across Generations
section: Why does a prospective member play with us three times first?
text:
Why does a prospective member play with us three times first?
Joining the club is deliberately not immediate.
A prospective member first attends at least three monthly meetings as a guest. After that, the person needs recommendations from at least two existing members and approval by two-thirds of the operating committee.
It may sound rather formal for a tennis club. There is a reason.
Three meetings are enough for the guest to decide whether this is a club he or she actually enjoys. They also give existing members time to play, eat, talk, and get to know the person naturally.
Tennis ability matters, but we care at least as much about character, consideration for others, and the ability to build healthy relationships within the group.
A club made entirely of top-level players might be a formidable tennis team. That is not quite what we are trying to build.
Strong and developing players should be able to enjoy the same meeting. A member in his seventies and one in his twenties should be able to become doubles partners. We should not become a professors’ club, nor should one company or institution dominate the membership.
Keeping different people comfortably mixed together is itself part of running the club.
Recently, looking at some of our younger new members, another possible membership criterion has been suggested.
“Do you also screen for good looks?”
For the record, that one is not in the bylaws.






Figure 7: With some of our newer members. Good looks are not a membership requirement—at least not officially.

title: KSCE FIRE DRAGONS: How Tennis Connects Civil Engineers Across Generations
section: Tennis as a bridge between civil engineering organizations
text:
Tennis as a bridge between civil engineering organizations
In recent years, we have placed more emphasis on inter-organizational exchange matches.
We have played with civil engineering tennis groups in the Jeonnam region and expanded friendly matches with clubs at other organizations. In June 2026, for example, we visited the Korea Expressway Corporation headquarters for an exchange match. Our side included members from universities, engineering firms, construction companies, and public organizations, while engineers from several departments of the Korea Expressway Corporation joined from their side.
It would be dishonest to say that winning does not matter. Once people walk onto a court, they want to win.
The interesting part comes afterward.
After the match we shake hands, eat together, and talk. Something lasts longer than the score: you now know the person on the other side of the net.
Civil engineers already have many formal networks—conferences, technical committees, clients, designers, contractors, and joint projects. Tennis creates a different connection. We often get to know the person first and only later learn the title, university, company, or institution attached to the name.
I think this kind of natural and healthy network among civil engineers is an important role for the club.

title: KSCE FIRE DRAGONS: How Tennis Connects Civil Engineers Across Generations
section: From a president-and-secretary club to a shared organization
text:
From a president-and-secretary club to a shared organization
As membership and activities expanded, the way we ran the club also had to change.
In the early years, the president and secretary handled most things. Once membership exceeded thirty and the number of events and exchange matches increased, I did not think that model was sustainable.
After becoming president, I therefore strengthened an operating committee system. Members now share responsibilities such as communications, external relations, and membership management, and important matters are discussed together.
This is more than distributing work.
If a club works only because one president or one secretary works very hard, it becomes fragile the moment that person leaves.
People change. The culture should remain.

title: KSCE FIRE DRAGONS: How Tennis Connects Civil Engineers Across Generations
text:
And now, 2026
On October 3, 2026, we held the KSCE President’s Cup at the Seoul National University of Science and Technology faculty tennis courts.






Figure 8: The 2026 KSCE President’s Cup on October 3, 2026. Different generations, organizations, and levels of play—but on the court, everyone is simply a tennis player. This is KSCE FIRE DRAGONS today.



Friendship is important, but we are still tennis players. Once the match starts, things become serious.






Figure 9: Friendship matters. Once the match starts, however, that is a different story. Awards at the 2026 KSCE President’s Cup.



And tennis has one very important fundamental.
Watch the ball all the way.






Figure 10: One of the fundamentals of tennis is to watch the ball all the way. Follow that advice too faithfully, however, and your eyes may look as if they are about to pop out.

title: KSCE FIRE DRAGONS: How Tennis Connects Civil Engineers Across Generations
section: What I hope remains for the next generation of FIRE DRAGONS
text:
What I hope remains for the next generation of FIRE DRAGONS
Our nickname is KSCE FIRE DRAGONS.
What began with a few people in 2012 has become a club of 34 dues-paying members. But I do not think membership count is the best measure of what we have built.
The real asset accumulated over nearly fifteen years is people.
People who can play together across age and rank. People who can take care of a less experienced partner. People from different organizations who can meet comfortably because they share civil engineering—and tennis.
When I became president in 2022, I wanted to make the character of the club a little clearer: diversity in generation and playing level; balance among professions and organizations; a culture of character and consideration; shared operation through the committee; and a wider, healthy network of civil engineers through institutional exchanges.
My term as president is coming to an end.
Presidents change. I hope that culture does not.
A tennis ball crosses the net, people become closer, and those relationships in turn connect our civil engineering community. I hope KSCE FIRE DRAGONS continues to connect senior and junior engineers, universities and industry, public agencies and private companies, regions and institutions—for many years to come.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
text:
English | 한글
A jacket-supported offshore wind turbine looks familiar to a structural engineer.
There is a tower.
Below it is a three-dimensional steel frame composed of tubular legs and braces.
Below that are piles embedded in the seabed.
It is tempting to idealize the whole system as
\[
\text{tower}
\rightarrow
\text{frame members}
\rightarrow
\text{fixed support}.
\]
Then structural stiffness appears to be determined mainly by familiar member properties such as
\[
EA
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
EI.
\]
But a real jacket-supported offshore wind turbine is more complicated.
The tower load must first be redistributed through a transition piece. The tubular braces connect to chord walls that deform locally. Finally, the piles themselves deform together with the surrounding soil.
A more realistic structural chain is therefore
\[
\boxed{
\text{Tower}
\rightarrow
\text{Transition piece}
\rightarrow
\text{Tubular joints}
\rightarrow
\text{Jacket members}
\rightarrow
\text{Piles}
\rightarrow
\text{Soil}
}
\]
Every part of this chain contributes to the response.
This leads to a useful engineering question:
Two of our studies approached this question from different scales.
The first investigated how the transition piece transfers loads from the tower into the jacket.
The second examined how local joint flexibility and pile-soil interaction change the dynamic response of the entire offshore wind turbine. :contentReferenceoaicite:0
Together, they reveal a broader structural principle:

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
text:
Start with the load path
Before discussing stiffness, consider what the structure actually has to do.
Wind acting on the rotor and tower produces forces and large overturning moments.
Those actions must travel downward:
\[
\text{Rotor}
\rightarrow
\text{Tower}
\rightarrow
\text{Transition piece}
\rightarrow
\text{Jacket}
\rightarrow
\text{Foundation}
\rightarrow
\text{Ground}.
\]
The tower and jacket, however, have very different geometries.
The tower is essentially a single large tubular shell.
The jacket consists of spatially separated legs connected by braces.
The transition piece therefore has to transform the forces and moments carried by one structural system into forces that can be carried by another.
This is the first important interface.



A jacket-supported offshore wind turbine. The transition piece connects the single tubular tower to the spatially separated jacket legs, while the piles continue below the seabed into the soil.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: The transition piece is a load-distribution structure
text:
The transition piece is a load-distribution structure
Unlike a monopile-supported turbine, a jacket-supported offshore wind turbine requires a special structural region between the tower and jacket.
The tower load must be redistributed through this transition piece because of the large geometric difference between the tower and the jacket.
Our transition-piece study therefore treated the ability of the transition piece to redistribute and transfer forces from the tower as a central determinant of structural performance.
Several transition-piece concepts were investigated numerically, including brace-type, box-girder-type, composite-plate-type, and single-web-type configurations.
But the most interesting lesson was not which configuration ranked first.
It was what the stress distributions revealed about load transfer.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: High stress can reveal a poor load path
text:
High stress can reveal a poor load path
Consider a conventional brace-type transition piece.
In the basic configuration, the maximum stress reached approximately
\[
329~\text{MPa}.
\]
More revealing than the magnitude was its location.
The maximum stress occurred in the tower can wall, rather than in the brace or deck.
This indicated that the brace was not effectively redistributing and transmitting the tower load downward into the jacket.
The tower can was still carrying too much of the action.
A reinforcing ring was then added near the brace-can connection.
The maximum can-wall stress fell from approximately
\[
329~\text{MPa}
\]
to
\[
187~\text{MPa}.
\]
But a new stress concentration appeared around the brace-can-reinforcing-ring connection.
Why?
Because the reinforcement had changed the load path.
Part of the load previously carried primarily through the tower can was now being transferred into the brace.
This is an important way to interpret finite-element stress contours:

A stress concentration is often telling us where the load is being forced to change direction or transfer between components.




Evolution of the brace-type transition piece. The stress contours show that reinforcement does more than reduce a numerical maximum: it changes how load is transferred from the tower can through the braces toward the jacket legs.


The study subsequently modified the brace and its connection geometry to improve downward load transfer.
In one configuration, the maximum brace and deck stresses decreased by approximately 19.6% and 18.4%, respectively.
But making the tubular brace still larger did not continue this improvement.
The larger configuration produced higher brace stress and greater structural weight.
So,
\[
\boxed{
\text{more material}
\not\Rightarrow
\text{better load transfer}.
}
\]
The geometry of the load path matters.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: But load transfer is only the beginning
text:
But load transfer is only the beginning
Suppose we have designed an efficient transition piece.
We could now construct a global frame model of the jacket using beam elements.
At first glance, the structural problem appears straightforward.
Each member contributes familiar axial and bending stiffness:
\[
EA
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
EI.
\]
But this contains a hidden assumption.
What happens where one tubular member meets another?
In a conventional frame model, the brace and chord are often connected by an ideal rigid joint.
The member axes meet, and compatibility is enforced at the connection.
The mathematical joint has no deformation of its own.
The real tubular joint does.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: A tubular joint is not a mathematical point
text:
A tubular joint is not a mathematical point
Consider a brace welded to a larger tubular chord.
When the brace transmits force and moment into the chord, the chord wall deforms locally.
The connection therefore has its own compliance.
If the undeformed angle between members is \(\theta_0\), an ideal rigid-joint model essentially preserves that joint geometry:
\[
\theta_R=\theta_0.
\]
A real flexible tubular joint can deform so that
\[
\theta_F\neq\theta_0.
\]
This deformation is called local joint flexibility (LJF).
The 2024 study considered three ways of representing the brace-chord connection:

rigid joint,
center-to-center (CTC) joint,
local joint flexibility (LJF) model. :contentReferenceoaicite:1




Three representations of a tubular chord-brace joint: rigid, center-to-center (CTC), and local joint flexibility (LJF). The LJF model allows the chord wall to deform locally, introducing a deformation mechanism that an ideal rigid frame joint suppresses.


The rigid model suppresses local chord deformation.
The CTC model extends the brace axis to the chord centerline but still cannot accurately represent the detailed flexible response of the tubular joint.
The LJF model introduces the local compliance associated with the actual chord-brace connection. :contentReferenceoaicite:2
This seems like a local modeling detail.
But its influence is global.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: Local flexibility changes the whole turbine
text:
Local flexibility changes the whole turbine
For a vibrating structure, the natural frequencies follow the familiar eigenvalue problem
\[
\left(
\mathbf{K}
-
\omega^2\mathbf{M}
\right)\boldsymbol{\phi}
=
\mathbf{0}.
\]
The important quantity here is not simply the stiffness of each individual member.
It is the stiffness matrix of the entire assembled system:
\[
\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{system}}.
\]
If local joint deformation is suppressed, the assembled structure becomes artificially stiff.
That changes
\[
\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{system}},
\]
which changes
\[
\omega,
\]
and therefore changes the predicted natural frequency
\[
f=\frac{\omega}{2\pi}.
\]
The 2024 study showed exactly this behavior.
The rigid-joint model produced a first natural frequency of
\[
0.324~\text{Hz},
\]
while the LJF model gave
\[
0.301~\text{Hz}.
\]
Compared with the LJF model, the rigid and CTC models predicted maximum transition-piece fore-aft displacements that were respectively 19.79% and 16.38% lower.
At the same time, their predicted maximum member stresses were 54.12% and 32.08% higher than those obtained using the LJF model. :contentReferenceoaicite:3
So neglecting local joint deformation does not introduce one simple conservative error.
It changes different response quantities in different ways.
A model can be conservative for stress while simultaneously being non-conservative for displacement.
That distinction is important.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: Then we reach another interface: the seabed
text:
Then we reach another interface: the seabed
Even if the tubular joints are modeled correctly, another simplification remains.
Where does the jacket end?
A convenient structural model may place a fixed boundary at the seabed:
\[
u=0,
\qquad
\theta=0.
\]
But a pile does not actually stop at the mudline.
It continues into the soil.
Under lateral loading, the pile bends and the surrounding soil deforms.
The foundation therefore contributes another source of flexibility.
This is pile-soil interaction.
The 2024 study compared four foundation representations:

fixed foundation (FF),
equivalent coupled springs (ECS),
apparent fixity length (AFL),
distributed nonlinear springs (DNS). :contentReferenceoaicite:4

The DNS model represents soil resistance using nonlinear springs distributed along the pile and was used as the higher-fidelity reference for comparison.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: Foundation modeling changes the predicted dynamics
text:
Foundation modeling changes the predicted dynamics
Using the DNS model as reference, the fixed-foundation model predicted a first natural frequency of
\[
0.304~\text{Hz},
\]
compared with
\[
0.283~\text{Hz}
\]
for DNS.
That is a 7.42% increase.
The equivalent coupled-spring model gave a similar overestimate of 7.07%. :contentReferenceoaicite:5
The difference in displacement was even larger.
The maximum transition-piece fore-aft displacement was
\[
0.130~\text{m}
\]
for the fixed-foundation model and
\[
0.189~\text{m}
\]
for the DNS model.
Thus, the fixed-foundation assumption underestimated the displacement by 31.36% relative to DNS.
The apparent-fixity-length model behaved in the opposite direction for some quantities.
Its maximum displacement and member stress were respectively 12.42% and 10.70% higher than those from the DNS model. :contentReferenceoaicite:6
This is another important lesson.
There is no universal correction such as

“A fixed foundation is always conservative.”

It depends on which response quantity is being examined.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: Joint flexibility and foundation flexibility act together
text:
Joint flexibility and foundation flexibility act together
The most revealing comparison comes when both effects are considered simultaneously.
Four models were compared:



Model
Joint
Foundation




Rigid & FF
Rigid
Fixed


LJF & FF
Flexible
Fixed


Rigid & DNS
Rigid
Flexible


LJF & DNS
Flexible
Flexible



The LJF & DNS model represents both local joint flexibility and pile-soil flexibility and was used as the higher-fidelity reference.



Combined influence of joint and foundation modeling on global structural response. Accounting for both local joint flexibility (LJF) and distributed pile-soil interaction (DNS) changes the predicted natural frequency, transition-piece displacement, and member stress, showing how local deformation mechanisms propagate into global dynamics.


The corresponding results were: :contentReferenceoaicite:7









Model
First natural frequency
Maximum TP displacement
Maximum member stress




Rigid & FF
0.324 Hz

LJF & FF
0.301 Hz

52.848 MPa



Relative to LJF & DNS, the completely rigidized Rigid & FF model predicted a first natural frequency 16.13% higher and a maximum transition-piece displacement 42.30% lower. :contentReferenceoaicite:8
This is too large to dismiss as a small modeling detail.
The model is describing a substantially different mechanical system.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: Why do many small flexibilities matter so much?
text:
Why do many small flexibilities matter so much?
The reason becomes clearer if we stop thinking of the jacket as a collection of beam elements and instead think of it as a sequence of deformable structural regions.
Very schematically,
\[
\text{tower}
-
\text{TP}
-
\text{joint}
-
\text{member}
-
\text{joint}
-
\text{pile}
-
\text{soil}.
\]
Under a generalized load \(F\), the total displacement can be viewed conceptually as
\[
u_{\mathrm{total}}
=
u_{\mathrm{TP}}
+
u_{\mathrm{members}}
+
u_{\mathrm{joints}}
+
u_{\mathrm{foundation}}.
\]
This is not intended as a literal decomposition for a three-dimensional coupled jacket system.
It is a useful mechanical picture.
If a numerical model assumes
\[
u_{\mathrm{joints}}=0
\]
and
\[
u_{\mathrm{foundation}}=0,
\]
the total displacement becomes smaller.
The corresponding effective stiffness,
\[
k_{\mathrm{eff}}
\sim
\frac{F}{u_{\mathrm{total}}},
\]
becomes larger.
The natural frequency then tends to increase because, schematically,
\[
f
\propto
\sqrt{\frac{k_{\mathrm{eff}}}{m}}.
\]
So the change in natural frequency is not mysterious.
The simplified model has removed real deformation mechanisms from the system.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: The critical flexibility may be concentrated at interfaces
text:
The critical flexibility may be concentrated at interfaces
This leads to a broader structural observation.
The long tubular members are visually dominant.
But they are not necessarily where the most important modeling uncertainty resides.
Significant deformation mechanisms can be concentrated at
\[
\boxed{
\text{interfaces}
}
\]
such as

tower-transition-piece load transfer,
brace-chord joints,
pile-soil interaction.

The transition-piece study showed that changing local geometry can substantially alter how load flows from the tower into the jacket.
The later dynamic study showed that allowing local chord deformation and pile-soil deformation changes the stiffness and dynamic response of the entire turbine. :contentReferenceoaicite:9
These results operate at different scales, but they tell the same mechanical story.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: Local mechanics can control global dynamics
text:
Local mechanics can control global dynamics
This is perhaps the most important connection between the two studies.
The transition-piece problem initially appears local:

How should the tower load enter the jacket?

The tubular-joint problem also appears local:

How much does the chord wall deform when a brace transfers load into it?

Pile-soil interaction likewise appears to be a foundation detail:

How does the pile deform against the surrounding soil?

But each local mechanism contributes to global flexibility.
And global flexibility determines dynamic properties such as
\[
f_n,
\qquad
u(t),
\qquad
\sigma(t).
\]
Thus,
\[
\boxed{
\text{local load transfer}
\rightarrow
\text{local deformation}
\rightarrow
\text{global stiffness}
\rightarrow
\text{global dynamic response}
}
\]
This is why seemingly small modeling decisions at joints and foundations can alter predictions for the entire offshore wind turbine.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: Why this matters especially for offshore wind turbines
text:
Why this matters especially for offshore wind turbines
For many conventional structures, a moderate error in natural frequency may not dominate design.
Offshore wind turbines are different.
They operate continuously under cyclic aerodynamic and hydrodynamic excitation.
The structural natural frequencies must therefore be considered relative to excitation frequencies associated with rotor rotation and blade passing.
In the 2024 study, the rotor rotational-frequency range was approximately
\[
0.115\text{--}0.202~\text{Hz},
\]
while the blade-passing range was approximately
\[
0.345\text{--}0.606~\text{Hz}.
\]
The rigid-joint model produced a first natural frequency of
\[
0.324~\text{Hz},
\]
placing it close to the blade-passing-frequency region considered in the analysis.
Accounting for both LJF and DNS foundation flexibility reduced the corresponding first natural frequency to
\[
0.279~\text{Hz}.
\]
Thus, modeling flexibility can change not only calculated displacement and stress.
It can alter the engineer’s interpretation of the dynamic separation between structural and excitation frequencies. :contentReferenceoaicite:10

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
text:
Simplification is not the problem
This does not mean that every jacket offshore wind turbine should always be modeled using detailed shell elements, full three-dimensional soil continua, and highly expensive nonlinear simulations.
Engineering analysis necessarily uses idealization.
The real question is:

Which deformation mechanisms can safely be simplified, and which ones control the response we care about?

Frame elements remain extremely useful because they make analysis of large jacket structures computationally efficient.
Simplified foundation models can also be appropriate.
The 2024 study itself examined simplified models precisely because practical engineering requires them. It further found that different simplified models behave differently as soil and pile stiffness change. :contentReferenceoaicite:11
The important point is to understand what each simplification removes.
A rigid joint removes local chord deformation.
A fixed foundation removes pile-soil deformation.
A simplified transition piece may remove the actual mechanism by which tower loads are redistributed into the jacket legs.
If those deformation mechanisms are important to the response quantity being studied, the simplification becomes important too.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
text:
Stiffness is a system property
Structural engineers often associate stiffness with a member property:
\[
EA,
\qquad
EI,
\qquad
GJ.
\]
These quantities are fundamental.
But the offshore jacket example reminds us that global structural stiffness is not obtained from member stiffness alone.
It emerges from the assembled system:
\[
\boxed{
\text{Global stiffness}
=
\text{members}
+
\text{connections}
+
\text{load-transfer regions}
+
\text{foundation interaction}.
}
\]
This is a conceptual statement rather than a literal additive stiffness equation.
Its purpose is to emphasize where deformation can occur.
A sophisticated beam model with perfectly rigid joints and perfectly fixed foundations may therefore be less representative than a relatively simple model that captures the dominant flexibility mechanisms correctly.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
section: What should an engineer look for?
text:
What should an engineer look for?
When constructing or reviewing a jacket offshore wind turbine model, it is useful to ask:
How does the tower load enter the jacket?
Is the transition-piece geometry providing a rational load path, or is stress being forced through localized regions?
Are the tubular joints really rigid?
If local chord-wall deformation contributes significantly to the response, a rigid beam intersection may overestimate stiffness.
Where is the foundation assumed to be fixed?
Does that boundary condition represent the actual pile-soil system sufficiently well for the response being investigated?
Which response quantity matters?
Natural frequency, displacement, member stress, and fatigue may respond differently to the same modeling simplification.
This last point is particularly important.
A modeling assumption that appears conservative for one quantity can be non-conservative for another.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
text:
Limitations
The results discussed here come from two specific numerical studies and should not be interpreted as universal correction factors for all jacket-supported offshore wind turbines.
The transition-piece study used an NREL 5-MW reference turbine and a specific jacket geometry and environmental condition. The structural comparisons were made for the particular transition-piece concepts examined in that study.
The joint- and foundation-flexibility study likewise used a specific 5-MW jacket-supported OWT, soil profile, environmental conditions, joint formulations, and foundation models. It also simplified the turbine-blade-hub system as a lumped mass and represented aerodynamic loading in simplified form. :contentReferenceoaicite:12
Therefore, values such as
\[
16.13\%,
\qquad
42.30\%,
\]
should not be applied as general correction factors.
Their importance is conceptual:

Neglected interface flexibility can be large enough to materially change the predicted response of the entire structure.

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
text:
Engineering takeaway
A jacket offshore wind turbine is easy to draw as a frame.
But mechanically, it is a chain of load-transfer and deformation mechanisms:
\[
\text{Tower}
\rightarrow
\text{Transition piece}
\rightarrow
\text{Tubular joints}
\rightarrow
\text{Jacket members}
\rightarrow
\text{Piles}
\rightarrow
\text{Soil}.
\]
The members matter.
But so do the places where the members meet, where the load changes its path, and where the structure enters the ground.
That leads to the central engineering principle:

The members are not the whole structure. The interfaces are part of the stiffness too.

And when a numerical model appears unexpectedly stiff, the first question should not always be:

Are the members too large?

It may be more useful to ask:

Which real deformation mechanism did the model remove?

title: Where Does the Flexibility of a Jacket-Supported Offshore Wind Turbine Really Come From?
text:
Original research
