title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
text:
English | 한글
A floating structure is both a structure and a body moving in water.
Waves apply pressure to the structure. Wind may add aerodynamic loading. But the interaction does not stop there.
Once the structure moves, its motion changes the surrounding fluid field. The resulting fluid pressure acts back on the structure.
That is the essence of fluid–structure interaction.
For a flexible floating body, the central engineering question is:
The frequency-domain formulation provides a particularly clear answer because every contribution can be separated into familiar dynamic roles:
The key idea is this:

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
text:
Start from ordinary structural dynamics
Before considering hydrodynamics, begin with a standard structural dynamic equation,
\[
\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{u}}
+
\mathbf{C}\dot{\mathbf{u}}
+
\mathbf{K}\mathbf{u}
=
\mathbf{f}.
\]
Here,

\(\mathbf{M}\) is the structural mass matrix,
\(\mathbf{C}\) is the structural damping matrix,
\(\mathbf{K}\) is the structural stiffness matrix,
and \(\mathbf{f}\) is the external force vector.

For a floating structure, the external force includes pressure acting on the wetted surface.
From the principle of virtual work,
\[
\delta W_{\mathrm{kin}}
=
\delta W_{\mathrm{ext}}
-
\delta W_{\mathrm{int}}.
\]
The inertia term is
\[
\delta W_{\mathrm{kin}}
=
\int_\Omega
\rho_s \delta \mathbf{u}\cdot\ddot{\mathbf{u}}
\,d\Omega,
\]
the external work includes gravity and fluid pressure,
\[
\delta W_{\mathrm{ext}}
=
-\int_\Omega
\delta\mathbf{u}\cdot\rho_s g\mathbf{e}_3
\,d\Omega
+
\int_{\Gamma_w}
p\,\delta\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{n}
\,d\Gamma,
\]
and the internal work is
\[
\delta W_{\mathrm{int}}
=
\int_\Omega
\delta\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}:
\mathbf{C}:
\boldsymbol{\varepsilon}
\,d\Omega.
\]
After spatial discretization, the familiar structural equation follows.
The important point is that the pressure \(p\) is not generally known in advance.
It depends on the fluid motion.






Figure 1: A flexible floating wind turbine subjected to waves and wind. The wetted surface transmits fluid pressure to the structure, while structural motion alters the surrounding flow. Mooring lines provide station keeping.



Figure Figure 1 shows the full physical problem.
The structure has its own mass and stiffness.
The fluid has its own dynamics.
The coupling occurs through pressure on the wetted surface.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
text:
Why modal coordinates are useful
For a flexible body, solving directly for every structural degree of freedom is possible but not always convenient.
A more compact description is obtained with structural eigenmodes:
\[
\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{X},t)
=
\sum_\alpha
\mathbf{\Psi}_\alpha(\mathbf{X})
\zeta_\alpha(t).
\]
Here,

\(\mathbf{\Psi}_\alpha\) is structural mode \(\alpha\),
\(\zeta_\alpha\) is its modal amplitude.

The structural matrices are then projected into modal space:
\[
M^*_{\alpha\beta}
=
\mathbf{\Psi}_\alpha^T
\mathbf{M}
\mathbf{\Psi}_\beta,
\]
\[
K^*_{\alpha\beta}
=
\mathbf{\Psi}_\alpha^T
\mathbf{K}
\mathbf{\Psi}_\beta.
\]
Similarly, the external force becomes a modal force,
\[
f^*_\alpha
=
\mathbf{\Psi}_\alpha^T
\mathbf{f}.
\]
This is useful because the hydrodynamic problem can also be organized around the same structural modes.
Each structural mode has a corresponding fluid radiation problem.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: Harmonic motion turns the problem into algebra
text:
Harmonic motion turns the problem into algebra
Assume harmonic motion with angular frequency \(\omega\),
\[
\zeta_\alpha(t)
=
\xi_\alpha e^{i\omega t}.
\]
Then
\[
\dot{\zeta}_\alpha
=
i\omega\xi_\alpha e^{i\omega t},
\]
and
\[
\ddot{\zeta}_\alpha
=
-\omega^2\xi_\alpha e^{i\omega t}.
\]
The structural dynamic equation becomes
\[
\left[
-\omega^2\mathbf{M}^*
+
i\omega\mathbf{C}^*
+
\mathbf{K}^*
\right]
\boldsymbol{\xi}
=
\mathbf{f}^*.
\]
The time-domain differential equation has become a frequency-dependent linear algebraic equation.
This is the basic advantage of frequency-domain analysis.
For each \(\omega\), solve one complex linear system.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: The hydrodynamic pressure comes from a velocity potential
text:
The hydrodynamic pressure comes from a velocity potential
In linear potential-flow theory, the dynamic pressure is obtained from the linearized Bernoulli equation,
\[
p
=
-\rho_w
\left(
\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial t}
+
gX_3
\right).
\]
For harmonic motion,
\[
\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial t}
=
i\omega\phi,
\]
so
\[
p
=
-\rho_w
\left(
i\omega\phi
+
gX_3
\right).
\]
The velocity potential satisfies
\[
\nabla^2\phi=0
\]
in the fluid domain.
The crucial point is that \(\phi\) itself contains several different physical contributions.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: Incident, diffraction, and radiation potentials play different roles
text:
Incident, diffraction, and radiation potentials play different roles
The linear potential is decomposed as
\[
\phi
=
\left[
A(\phi_I+\phi_D)
+
\xi_\alpha\phi_\alpha
\right]
e^{i\omega t},
\]
where

\(\phi_I\) is the incident-wave potential,
\(\phi_D\) is the diffraction potential,
\(\phi_\alpha\) is the radiation potential associated with structural mode \(\alpha\),
\(A\) is wave amplitude,
and \(\xi_\alpha\) is the structural modal response.

This decomposition is the physical heart of frequency-domain hydroelasticity.






Figure 2: The fluid problem separates naturally into two parts. Incident and diffracted waves create wave excitation even if the body is fixed. Structural motion generates radiation waves, and those radiated waves feed back on the structure as added mass and hydrodynamic damping.



Figure Figure 2 makes the distinction explicit.

Incident and diffraction problem
Imagine the body is held fixed while waves arrive.
The incident wave is disturbed by the body geometry and produces a scattered or diffracted wave.
The associated pressure produces the wave excitation force,
\[
\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{ex}}.
\]
This force exists even if the body does not move.


Radiation problem
Now imagine there is no incident wave, but the body is forced to oscillate.
Its motion generates waves in the surrounding fluid.
Those radiated waves react back on the body.
This reaction produces two familiar dynamic effects:

added inertia,
damping.

These are not arbitrary correction terms.
They are the mechanical consequence of the body having to accelerate and radiate part of the surrounding fluid.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: Added mass is fluid inertia seen by the structure
text:
Added mass is fluid inertia seen by the structure
When a body accelerates in water, it must also accelerate some surrounding fluid.
The body therefore behaves as if its inertia were larger than its dry structural mass.
In modal form, this contribution appears as the added-mass matrix,
\[
\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{hydro}}(\omega).
\]
The inertia term becomes
\[
-\omega^2
\left(
\mathbf{M}^*
+
\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\right)
\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\]
An important subtlety is that added mass can depend on frequency.
The effective inertia of the coupled fluid–structure system is therefore not necessarily constant.
This is one reason floating-body dynamics can differ substantially from dry structural dynamics.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: Radiation damping is energy carried away by waves
text:
Radiation damping is energy carried away by waves
An oscillating body radiates waves.
Those waves carry energy away from the structure.
To the structural system, that energy loss appears as damping.
The corresponding hydrodynamic damping matrix is
\[
\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{hydro}}(\omega).
\]
Its contribution is
\[
i\omega
\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\]
The physical interpretation is simple:

Radiation damping is the resistance associated with sending wave energy away from the oscillating body.

This is distinct from structural damping.
Structural damping represents dissipation inside the structure.
Radiation damping represents energy transfer from structure to fluid waves.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
text:
Hydrostatic pressure provides restoring stiffness
Gravity and buoyancy establish the equilibrium position of the floating body.
A small displacement changes the submerged geometry and therefore changes the hydrostatic pressure distribution.
Linearizing that effect produces a hydrostatic restoring matrix,
\[
\mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{hydro}}.
\]
Its contribution enters like stiffness:
\[
\mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\boldsymbol{\xi}.
\]
So water contributes not only inertia and damping.
It also contributes restoring action.
That gives a very useful structural interpretation:
water surrounding the body
      ↓
added mass          → inertia
radiation damping   → damping
hydrostatic restoring → stiffness
wave diffraction    → excitation

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
text:
The coupled frequency-domain equation
Collecting structural and hydrodynamic contributions gives
\[
\left[
-\omega^2
\left(
\mathbf{M}^*
+
\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\right)
+
i\omega
\left(
\mathbf{C}^*
+
\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\right)
+
\left(
\mathbf{K}^*
+
\mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\right)
\right]
\boldsymbol{\xi}
=
A\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{ex}}.
\]
This equation has the same architecture as ordinary structural dynamics.
The difference is that the fluid modifies every major dynamic component.






Figure 3: The frequency-domain equation can be read exactly like a structural dynamic equation: inertia, damping, restoring action, and excitation. Structural and hydrodynamic contributions simply occupy the same mechanical roles.



Figure Figure 3 is the most useful way to read the equation.
Do not begin by memorizing hydrodynamic coefficients.
Begin by asking what mechanical role each term plays.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: Wind can enter the same framework
text:
Wind can enter the same framework
For a floating wind turbine, the rotor thrust depends on the relative velocity between the wind and the moving structure.
In one dimension,
\[
T(t)
=
\frac{1}{2}
\rho_a C_T A
\left[
v_{\mathrm{wind}}(t)
-
\dot{u}(t)
\right]^2.
\]
Decompose the wind speed into a mean and a fluctuation,
\[
v_{\mathrm{wind}}(t)
=
v_0+v_f(t).
\]
If both the fluctuation and structural velocity are small relative to the mean wind speed, the thrust can be linearized:
\[
T(t)
\approx
T_0
+
T_f(t)
-
T_{\dot u}(t).
\]
The three contributions have different meanings:

\(T_0\): mean static thrust,
\(T_f\): excitation from wind fluctuation,
\(T_{\dot u}\): motion-dependent aerodynamic force.

The mean term belongs in the static equilibrium problem.
The motion-dependent term behaves like additional damping in the frequency-domain dynamic equation.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
text:
The full wave–wind system
Including the linearized wind interaction, the modal equation becomes
\[
\left[
-\omega^2
\left(
\mathbf{M}^*
+
\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\right)
+
i\omega
\left(
\mathbf{C}^*
+
\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
+
\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{wind}}
\right)
+
\left(
\mathbf{K}^*
+
\mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\right)
\right]
\boldsymbol{\xi}
=
A\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{ex}}
+
\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{wind}}.
\]
This equation is useful because it preserves familiar mechanical structure.

Inertia
\[
-\omega^2
\left(
\mathbf{M}^*
+
\mathbf{A}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\right)
\]


Damping
\[
i\omega
\left(
\mathbf{C}^*
+
\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
+
\mathbf{B}^{\mathrm{wind}}
\right)
\]


Restoring action
\[
\mathbf{K}^*
+
\mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{hydro}}
\]


Excitation
\[
A\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{ex}}
+
\mathbf{f}^{\mathrm{wind}}.
\]
This is why frequency-domain fluid–structure interaction is conceptually much closer to ordinary structural dynamics than it first appears.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: What does the response amplitude mean?
text:
What does the response amplitude mean?
The solution
\[
\boldsymbol{\xi}(\omega)
\]
is complex.
Its magnitude gives the response amplitude.
Its phase gives the lag or lead relative to the harmonic excitation.
For rigid-body motions such as surge, heave, and pitch, these quantities lead naturally to response-amplitude operators.
For flexible structures, modal amplitudes can be transformed back into physical displacement fields through
\[
\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{X},t)
=
\sum_\alpha
\mathbf{\Psi}_\alpha(\mathbf{X})
\xi_\alpha e^{i\omega t}.
\]
So the same framework can describe both rigid-body motion and structural deformation.
That is why the method is properly described as hydroelastic rather than purely hydrodynamic.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: Why the frequency domain is so efficient
text:
Why the frequency domain is so efficient
The frequency-domain method is powerful when the system can be linearized.
For each wave frequency:

solve the hydrodynamic boundary-value problem,
obtain added mass, radiation damping, and excitation,
assemble the coupled dynamic matrix,
solve for the complex response amplitude.

There is no need to integrate every oscillation cycle through time.
This makes the method particularly attractive for:

response-amplitude operators,
parameter studies,
design screening,
modal interpretation,
frequency-by-frequency load assessment.

The structure of the solution is also highly transparent.
Each term can be interpreted mechanically.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: But the efficiency comes from assumptions
text:
But the efficiency comes from assumptions
The frequency-domain formulation relies on linearization.
Typically, it assumes:

small wave amplitude,
small structural motion,
linear structural behavior,
linearized hydrostatics,
linear potential flow,
harmonic decomposition,
and linearization of motion-dependent wind loading.

These assumptions are powerful because they transform the problem into a linear algebraic system.
But they also define the range of applicability.
Strong nonlinearities, large motions, highly nonlinear mooring response, slamming, viscous separation, and other strongly time-dependent effects may require a time-domain treatment.
This distinction leads naturally to the companion article on mooring-line dynamics.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
section: Why mooring stiffness still matters in a frequency-domain model
text:
Why mooring stiffness still matters in a frequency-domain model
A floating wind turbine subjected to mean or fluctuating horizontal loading must remain stationed.
Hydrostatic restoring alone does not necessarily provide sufficient horizontal stiffness in surge or sway.
Mooring systems therefore contribute restoring action and prevent rigid-body drift.
In a linear frequency-domain model, the mooring system is often introduced through an equivalent stiffness around the equilibrium position.
That is appropriate when the mooring response can be linearized.
But a real mooring line has its own:

mass,
changing geometry,
elasticity,
gravity,
buoyancy,
drag,
and dynamic response.

Once these effects matter, the mooring system is no longer merely a stiffness matrix.
That is the subject of the next article.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
text:
Connection to structural mechanics
The most useful way to understand frequency-domain hydroelasticity is not to treat it as a completely separate branch of mechanics.
Its structure is familiar:
\[
\text{inertia}
+
\text{damping}
+
\text{restoring action}
=
\text{excitation}.
\]
The fluid modifies each category.
The engineering challenge is to understand why each hydrodynamic term belongs where it does.
That interpretation is more durable than memorizing coefficient names.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
text:
Engineering takeaway
A floating structure does not respond to waves as a dry structure with a wave force simply attached to it.
Its own motion generates fluid motion, and that fluid motion reacts back on the structure.
The result is a coupled system in which the surrounding water contributes:

inertia through added mass,
damping through wave radiation,
restoring action through hydrostatics,
and excitation through incident and diffracted waves.

So the principle to remember is:

The water is not merely an external load. Once the structure moves, the water becomes part of the dynamic system.

And the practical interpretation of the frequency-domain equation is:

Read hydrodynamic coefficients by their mechanical roles: inertia, damping, restoring action, and excitation.

title: How Does a Flexible Floating Structure Respond to Waves in the Frequency Domain?
text:
Next article
Why Is a Mooring Line More Than a Nonlinear Spring?
The companion article moves from the linearized frequency-domain model to time-domain mooring dynamics, where geometry, tension, drag, and line inertia evolve together.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
text:
Concrete durability is often taught as a collection of separate problems.
We study chloride ingress.
We study carbonation.
We study freezing and thawing.
We study alkali-silica reaction.
We study reinforcement corrosion.
This separation is useful in the classroom and often unavoidable in laboratory testing.
But real concrete does not know which chapter of the textbook we are studying.
A concrete structure experiences mechanical deformation, moisture transport, ion migration, gas diffusion, chemical reactions, hydration, dissolution and precipitation of solids, corrosion, and cracking at the same time.
More importantly, these processes interact.
A crack changes transport.
Transport changes chemical reaction.
Chemical reaction changes pore structure.
Pore structure changes transport again.
Reaction products may expand and generate stress.
Stress creates more cracks.
That is why concrete durability becomes much more difficult than solving several independent diffusion problems.
For more than a decade, a significant part of my research has dealt with different pieces of this coupled problem—from carbonation and chloride ingress to reinforcement corrosion and alkali-silica reaction (ASR). I remain interested in it because the central difficulty has not disappeared:
This article explains why that statement matters.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: The traditional picture is too simple
text:
The traditional picture is too simple
A simple durability model often starts with something like Fickian diffusion:
\[
\frac{\partial C}{\partial t}
=
\nabla \cdot \left(D\nabla C\right),
\]
where \(C\) is the concentration of a transported species and \(D\) is a diffusion coefficient.
This equation is extremely useful.
But what exactly is \(D\)?
If the pore structure changes because of carbonation, hydration, precipitation, dissolution, or cracking, the diffusion coefficient should change.
And what exactly is being transported?
Chloride may exist as free chloride in the pore solution or may be chemically bound. Carbonation can change that binding capacity and release previously bound chloride. Moisture changes the pathways available to gases and ions. Temperature changes reaction and transport rates.
Even the threshold for reinforcement depassivation may evolve as the chemical condition of the pore solution changes.
So the actual problem is closer to
environment
    ↓
moisture / ions / gases / heat
    ↓
transport through pores
    ↓
chemical and electrochemical reactions
    ↓
solid formation, dissolution, and pore-structure change
    ↓
stress, strain, expansion, and cracking
    ↓
new transport paths
    ↺
The last arrow is the important one.
The material through which diffusion occurs is itself changing.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: Example 1: carbonation and chloride ingress are not independent
text:
Example 1: carbonation and chloride ingress are not independent
Carbonation and chloride ingress provide a particularly clear example.
A conventional durability assessment may calculate a carbonation depth and a chloride profile independently and then compare each with a corrosion criterion.
That approach implicitly assumes that carbonation does not substantially change chloride transport.
But carbonation changes the chemistry and microstructure of concrete.
In our combined carbonation-chloride model, we considered coupled transport of carbon dioxide, chloride ions, moisture, and heat. Carbonation also changed the pore structure and chloride-binding capacity.
One particularly important mechanism is the decomposition of chloride-bearing Friedel’s salt during carbonation. Chloride that had been chemically bound can be released back into the pore solution.
Schematically,
\[
\text{bound chloride}
\;\xrightarrow{\text{carbonation}}\;
\text{free chloride in pore solution}.
\]
The significance is easy to miss if the two deterioration mechanisms are solved independently.
The chloride concentration is not governed only by chloride entering from the exposed surface. A chemical reaction occurring inside the concrete can create an internal source of free chloride.






Figure 1: Carbonation changes the chloride profile rather than simply advancing beside it. The upper plot shows how the carbonation front and free-chloride distribution vary with CO2 exposure. The lower plot shows the engineering consequence: in the illustrative calculation, coupling carbonation with chloride ingress moved the corrosion-initiation condition substantially earlier than the uncoupled treatment. Adapted from Zhu et al. (2016).



Figure Figure 1 illustrates the point.
The important observation is not merely that carbonation exists at the same time as chloride ingress.
It is that carbonation changes the chloride problem itself.
In the illustrative example in that study, the calculated corrosion-initiation time was reduced by about 40% when the combined mechanism was considered.
That result has a broader engineering meaning:

When one deterioration process changes the state variables governing another process, adding two independent predictions is not enough.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: A coupled durability problem needs state variables, not labels
text:
A coupled durability problem needs state variables, not labels
The words carbonation, chloride ingress, ASR, and corrosion are useful names for recognizable deterioration phenomena.
But computationally, it is often more useful to think in terms of evolving state variables.
For example:

moisture content or relative humidity,
temperature,
carbon dioxide concentration,
free and bound chloride,
oxygen concentration,
alkali concentration,
calcium concentration,
pH,
degree of carbonation,
porosity,
characteristic pore size,
reaction-product content,
corrosion current,
mechanical damage,
strain and stress.

The deterioration label is then an emergent result of interactions among these variables.
This way of thinking is familiar in mechanics.
A structural engineer does not usually say that equilibrium, constitutive behavior, and compatibility are three unrelated structural problems. They are different parts of one mechanical system.
Durability should often be viewed in the same way.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: Example 2: corrosion creates the crack that accelerates corrosion
text:
Example 2: corrosion creates the crack that accelerates corrosion
After reinforcement depassivation, the coupling becomes even stronger.
Corrosion is an electrochemical process. Iron dissolves, oxygen participates in cathodic reactions, corrosion products form, and the rust occupies a larger effective volume than the consumed steel.
That expansion generates pressure on the surrounding concrete.
Once cracking starts, the transport problem changes.
The cracked concrete provides easier pathways for moisture, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and chloride ions.
Therefore the sequence is not simply
chloride
→ corrosion
→ crack
but rather
chloride / carbonation
→ depassivation
→ electrochemical corrosion
→ rust expansion
→ cracking
→ faster transport
→ changed corrosion
→ further cracking
This is a genuine feedback loop.
In our two-dimensional mechano-chemical corrosion model, mass transport, carbonation, electrochemical reactions, rust expansion, and concrete cracking were coupled. The anode region was not fixed in advance; it developed as local chemical conditions changed.






Figure 2: The calculated free-chloride concentration and degree of carbonation after 40 years change when corrosion-induced mechanical damage is included. The comparison demonstrates the feedback direction that is often missing from durability analysis: damage is not only the result of transport—it changes subsequent transport. Adapted from Zhu and Zi (2017).



Figure Figure 2 is, to me, one of the clearest demonstrations of why durability must be treated as a coupled problem.
If cracking were only an output quantity, we could calculate transport first and mechanics later.
But once cracking modifies transport, the two calculations cannot remain one-way.
In the example studied, including mechanical damage substantially accelerated chloride arrival at parts of the reinforcement. At one reported location, the calculated corrosion-initiation time decreased from more than 60 years to about 28 years when the damage feedback was included.
The exact number belongs to that particular numerical example.
The general principle is more important:

Damage changes the environment experienced by the material inside the structure.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: Example 3: ASR requires chemistry, moisture, and mechanics in sequence
text:
Example 3: ASR requires chemistry, moisture, and mechanics in sequence
Alkali-silica reaction looks different from reinforcement corrosion, but it exposes the same multiphysics structure.
ASR begins with chemical attack on reactive silica.
Alkali participates in forming an ASR product. The product then imbibes water and swells. The swelling generates pressure on the surrounding solid skeleton. That pressure causes expansion and damage.
A useful conceptual sequence is
alkali transport
→ silica reaction
→ formation of basic ASR gel
→ water imbibition
→ gel swelling
→ expansive pressure
→ mechanical damage
In our chemo-mechanical ASR model, the formation of the basic gel and the swelling of the gel were deliberately separated.
The first is controlled primarily by the chemical availability of alkali.
The second requires moisture.
This distinction matters because the amount of reaction product and its swelling capacity are not the same physical quantity.






Figure 3: The ASR model tracks the progression of free alkali, reactive silica, basic ASR gel, free calcium, and C-S-H formed through alkali recycling. The figure emphasizes that durability is not governed by a single reaction front: several chemical fields and evolving solid phases coexist and interact. Adapted from Sun et al. (2020).



Figure Figure 3 shows this internal evolution at the scale of a reactive aggregate.
Calcium adds another level of coupling. Calcium entering the reacted layer can replace alkali and form C-S-H-like products. The chemical composition of the gel influences its capacity to swell.
Therefore ASR cannot be understood completely by asking only:

How fast does alkali diffuse?

We also need to ask:

How much reactive silica remains?
What reaction products form?
How much water reaches the gel?
What is the chemical composition of the product?
How much swelling can that product generate?
What stress does the swelling impose on the surrounding concrete?
How does the resulting damage alter subsequent transport?

The difficulty is not an excessively complicated equation.
The difficulty is that the material is changing across multiple scales.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: Hydration and nanoscale solid growth belong in the same picture
text:
Hydration and nanoscale solid growth belong in the same picture
Concrete begins evolving from the moment water contacts cement.
Hydration consumes water and unhydrated phases while creating new solids. These solids progressively construct the load-bearing skeleton and pore network.
Later durability reactions continue modifying that network.
Carbonation can dissolve or consume some phases and precipitate calcium carbonate.
ASR creates reaction products around or inside reactive aggregates.
Corrosion creates solid rust products at the steel-concrete interface.
At sufficiently small scales, durability is therefore inseparable from where solids grow, dissolve, and reorganize.
This is why a fixed value of porosity is often not enough.
Two concretes with the same total porosity can behave differently if their pore connectivity, pore-size distribution, saturation, and solid-phase distribution differ.
The important variable for transport is not simply how much empty space exists.
It is whether that space forms connected pathways.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: An apparent contradiction: carbonation can accelerate chloride damage—or improve chloride resistance
text:
An apparent contradiction: carbonation can accelerate chloride damage—or improve chloride resistance
Coupling also warns us against turning an observed mechanism into a universal rule.
Our earlier work on mature reinforced concrete showed how carbonation can accelerate chloride-related corrosion through changes in binding, pore structure, pH, and chloride release.
But accelerated carbonation can also be deliberately used at early age to densify some concrete systems.
In recent work on carbon-eating concrete incorporating electric-arc-furnace slag, accelerated carbonation produced calcium-carbonate-rich surface densification and reduced pore volume near the exposed surface. The carbonated specimens showed lower chloride penetration than their non-carbonated counterparts.






Figure 4: In the accelerated-carbonation study, both ordinary concrete and carbon-eating concrete showed reduced charge passage and chloride penetration depth after carbonation curing. This does not contradict the earlier combined-deterioration studies: the materials, age, exposure history, pore structure, and chemical state are different. Adapted from Lee et al. (2025).



This is an important reminder.
It would be wrong to conclude either

carbonation always makes chloride ingress worse

or

carbonation always improves chloride resistance.

The effect depends on the material state and the pathway by which that state was reached.
Early accelerated carbonation of a designed material can create dense reaction products and refine surface pores.
Long-term environmental carbonation of reinforced concrete can reduce alkalinity, modify chloride binding, release bound chloride, and contribute to reinforcement depassivation.
The word carbonation is the same.
The coupled state of the material is not.
This is exactly why mechanistic modeling is necessary.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
text:
Durability has several characteristic scales
Another source of difficulty is scale.
At the nanoscale and microscale, we may care about:

hydration products,
ion binding,
gel chemistry,
precipitation and dissolution,
pore geometry.

At the mesoscale, we may care about:

aggregates,
interfacial transition zones,
localized reaction,
distributed microcracking.

At the structural scale, we care about:

cover thickness,
exposure boundaries,
crack networks,
reinforcement layout,
corrosion initiation and propagation,
stiffness and load-carrying capacity,
service life and reliability.

A useful model does not necessarily resolve every scale explicitly.
That would often be computationally impossible.
The challenge is to decide which small-scale mechanisms must survive in the larger-scale model.
For example, we do not need to simulate every Friedel’s salt crystal to represent carbonation-induced release of bound chloride.
But the release mechanism may need to appear as a source term in the macroscopic mass balance.
Likewise, we do not need to model every ASR molecule.
But the model must distinguish formation of reaction product from moisture-driven swelling if those two processes control different aspects of the observed expansion.
This is model reduction with physical meaning.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: Why single-mechanism tests are still necessary
text:
Why single-mechanism tests are still necessary
None of this means that isolated durability tests are useless.
They are essential.
A chloride migration test can identify transport characteristics.
A carbonation test can characterize carbonation resistance.
An ASR expansion test can reveal aggregate reactivity.
A freeze-thaw test can compare mixture performance.
The problem occurs when we move from material characterization to service-life prediction and assume that the isolated mechanisms remain independent in the real structure.
Single-mechanism experiments help identify components of the problem.
Combined models ask how those components interact.
The distinction is important:
laboratory isolation
    helps us understand a mechanism

structural exposure
    requires us to understand interaction

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: Probability makes the coupling even more important
text:
Probability makes the coupling even more important
Durability parameters are uncertain.
Cover thickness varies.
Surface chloride concentration varies.
Humidity and temperature vary.
Diffusion coefficients vary.
Chemical threshold values vary.
Material composition varies.
For this reason, service-life prediction is naturally probabilistic.
But probabilistic analysis does not repair an incomplete physical model.
If the deterministic model assumes independent carbonation and chloride ingress when the mechanisms are actually coupled, adding sophisticated probability distributions only quantifies uncertainty around the wrong physical structure.
In our probabilistic study of combined carbonation and chloride ingress, the coupled calculation predicted a much higher probability of corrosion initiation than treating the mechanisms independently.
A later simplified probabilistic model was developed because the comprehensive coupled formulation was computationally expensive.
That progression is itself instructive:
understand the coupled physics
→ construct the comprehensive model
→ identify dominant variables
→ simplify without destroying the coupling
→ perform practical reliability analysis
This is usually safer than starting with a simple independent model and adding empirical correction factors without knowing which interactions matter.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: What should a future durability model contain?
text:
What should a future durability model contain?
There is no universal model that must include everything.
The appropriate level of coupling depends on the engineering question.
But for difficult long-term durability problems, I would think in terms of five interacting layers.

1. Mechanical fields
Stress, strain, deformation, cracking, and damage.


2. Transport fields
Moisture, heat, ions, gases, and sometimes electrical potential.


3. Chemical and electrochemical reactions
Carbonation, chloride binding and release, hydration, ASR chemistry, corrosion reactions, dissolution, and precipitation.


4. Evolving microstructure
Porosity, pore-size distribution, connectivity, reaction layers, newly formed solids, and damaged pathways.


5. Structural consequence
Reinforcement depassivation, corrosion loss, cracking, stiffness degradation, strength reduction, and probability of reaching an unacceptable state.
The key requirement is not to maximize the number of equations.
It is to retain the feedback loops that control the engineering outcome.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
section: My own route through this problem
text:
My own route through this problem
My work in this area has not followed a single deterioration mechanism.
The questions gradually moved across scales and couplings.
Early experimental work examined concrete exposed to combined freeze-thaw action and de-icing salts, including the influence of waste-glass sludge on strength, chloride penetration, scaling, and freeze-thaw resistance.
The carbonation-chloride studies then focused on why two major causes of reinforcement depassivation should not be treated independently.
That led naturally to probabilistic service-life analysis.
The corrosion work extended the chain beyond initiation:
transport
→ depassivation
→ electrochemistry
→ rust
→ expansive pressure
→ cracking
→ altered transport
The ASR studies approached another deterioration mechanism but again required transport, reaction, evolving solid products, water uptake, and mechanical damage.
More recent carbonation work has moved toward deliberately using reaction and microstructure evolution to improve performance rather than merely predict deterioration.
The common subject is therefore not chloride, carbonation, corrosion, ASR, glass, or slag individually.
It is the coupled evolution of concrete.
That is the research problem that still interests me.

title: Why Can’t We Study Concrete Durability One Mechanism at a Time?
text:
Engineering takeaway
The most important lesson is simple:

Concrete durability is not a collection of independent deterioration mechanisms. It is the coupled evolution of transport, reaction, microstructure, and mechanics.

A useful durability model therefore should not be judged primarily by how many mechanisms it contains.
It should be judged by whether it preserves the interactions that change the engineering answer.
When a chemical reaction changes transport, couple it.
When damage changes transport, couple it.
When moisture controls swelling, couple it.
When newly formed solids change pore connectivity, couple it.
And when the interaction is weak enough to ignore, demonstrate why.
That is how a complicated multiphysics problem becomes an engineering model rather than merely a large collection of equations.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
text:
English | 한글
Computational Fracture Series: Article 1 of 7 · Next: XFEM →
A crack creates a peculiar problem for computational mechanics.
Before cracking, we normally approximate a continuous displacement field over a body. After a crack appears, the displacement field can become discontinuous across an internal surface. The crack may then grow, turn, branch, join another crack, or cut through elements that were never designed to contain it.
The physical body changes its internal topology while the numerical mesh would prefer to remain unchanged.
That is the central difficulty.
I was very active in computational fracture for many years. Much of my work in this field involved the extended finite element method (XFEM) and its meshfree counterpart, the extended element-free Galerkin method (XEFG), together with dynamic fracture, cohesive cracks, multiple-crack growth, three-dimensional crack tracking, phantom-node formulations, and related methods.
Looking back, I think the most useful way to explain this work is not paper by paper.
The engineering question is:
That question connects a large part of the work.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: Why ordinary finite elements have difficulty with cracks
text:
Why ordinary finite elements have difficulty with cracks
In a standard finite element approximation,
\[
\mathbf{u}^h(\mathbf{x})
=
\sum_I N_I(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}_I,
\]
the interpolation is built from shape functions attached to the mesh.
This is extremely effective as long as the displacement field has the regularity assumed by the interpolation.
A crack changes that.
Across a crack surface, the displacement may jump:
\[
[\![\mathbf{u}]\!] \neq \mathbf{0}.
\]
Near a classical crack tip, the stress and strain fields can also contain strong gradients or singular asymptotic behavior.
If the crack is forced to follow element boundaries, the numerical representation becomes easy, but the mesh begins to influence the crack path.
If the crack is allowed to cut arbitrarily through elements, then the approximation must somehow represent a discontinuity that is not built into the original mesh connectivity.
Historically, one solution was remeshing:
grow crack
→ modify mesh
→ project state variables
→ solve again
→ grow crack
→ remesh again
This can work, but repeated remeshing is burdensome. It introduces projection between successive meshes, complicates history-dependent problems, and makes multiple cracks, branching, and dynamic propagation increasingly difficult.
The deeper idea behind XFEM was to avoid making the mesh carry all the geometric information about the crack.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: The key idea: separate the crack from the mesh
text:
The key idea: separate the crack from the mesh
The ordinary finite element space can be enriched with additional functions that contain information about the discontinuity.
A schematic enriched approximation is
\[
\mathbf{u}^h(\mathbf{x})
=
\sum_I N_I(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}_I
+
\sum_{J\in\mathcal{N}_c}
N_J(\mathbf{x})\Psi_J(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{a}_J,
\]
where the first term is the ordinary approximation and the second provides additional degrees of freedom associated with the crack.
The important feature is conceptual:
background mesh
    represents the body

enrichment
    represents information missing from the ordinary approximation
The crack is therefore allowed to pass through an element without requiring that the element boundary coincide with the crack.






Figure 1: A cohesive crack can be represented as an internal discontinuity inside a body, with the crack geometry described independently of the external boundary and loading. This separation between the physical discontinuity and the background discretization is the basis of the enriched viewpoint. Adapted from Zi and Belytschko (2003).



Figure Figure 1 looks simple, but it contains the essential shift in viewpoint.
The crack is an internal geometric object.
The mesh is a discretization device.
They do not have to be the same object.

Do not force the mesh to represent the crack. Give the approximation enough information to represent the crack independently of the mesh.

This became one of the most powerful ideas in computational fracture.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: Why the crack tip is more difficult than the crack interior
text:
Why the crack tip is more difficult than the crack interior
Representing a fully developed displacement jump is relatively straightforward.
The crack tip is harder.
Along the open part of the crack, the two sides are separated. At the tip, however, the crack opening must close properly.
This means that simply enriching every cut element with the same discontinuous function does not automatically produce the correct kinematics near the tip.
One of my early contributions with Ted Belytschko addressed precisely this issue for cohesive cracks.
Instead of treating the crack-tip element as an awkward exception that required the conventional branch-function construction, we developed new crack-tip formulations that allowed the crack to end inside an element while maintaining the required crack closure.
That work had a practical objective:

make arbitrary crack growth easier to implement while retaining a clean enriched representation.

This concern reappeared repeatedly in later methods, including XEFG and phantom-node formulations.
The crack interior is a discontinuity problem.
The crack tip is simultaneously a discontinuity-termination problem and a propagation problem.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: Crack geometry also has to move
text:
Crack geometry also has to move
Once the approximation can represent a crack, another question appears:

Where is the crack?

For a growing crack, the geometry itself must evolve.
Level-set descriptions became useful because the crack could be represented by nodal scalar fields rather than by constantly rebuilding mesh topology.
For example, one field can describe the signed distance normal to the crack and another can help locate the tip.
This creates an important separation:
finite element mesh
    ↓
approximation space

level-set or geometric representation
    ↓
crack position and crack tip

fracture criterion
    ↓
where the crack moves next
The numerical method therefore needs more than a stress calculation.
It needs a representation of evolving geometry.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: Dynamic fracture makes the problem even harder
text:
Dynamic fracture makes the problem even harder
In static crack growth, a crack may be advanced incrementally after checking a fracture criterion.
In dynamic fracture, the crack propagates while inertia is important.
Now several questions are coupled:

When does the crack start?
In which direction does it move?
How fast does it move?
How is cohesive energy dissipated?
How should the discontinuity be updated during time integration?
Can the crack path remain independent of the element orientation?

Our XFEM work on dynamic fracture used local partition-of-unity enrichment together with level sets so that arbitrary crack paths could be represented without remeshing.






Figure 2: A dynamic mixed-mode crack evolves through the fixed triangular mesh while the mesh itself remains unchanged. The important point is not the particular crack path, but that the crack geometry can advance independently of the element edges. Adapted from Zi et al. (2005).



Figure Figure 2 shows the numerical idea directly.
The crack moves.
The background mesh does not.
That may sound obvious today, but it addresses one of the most persistent practical problems in numerical fracture.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: Multiple cracks change the topology, not just the geometry
text:
Multiple cracks change the topology, not just the geometry
A single smooth crack is only the beginning.
Real fracture can involve:

several cracks initiating at different locations,
crack competition,
crack shielding,
coalescence,
branching,
crack junctions,
and eventually a connected fracture network.

In our work on multiple crack growth, XFEM was used together with implicit crack descriptions so that cracks could grow and interconnect without remeshing.
This is a much more demanding problem than advancing one crack tip.
When two cracks join, the topology of the discontinuity network changes.
A good numerical representation should not require a completely different algorithm every time that topology changes.
This is one reason enrichment-based approaches became attractive: the mesh can remain a background structure while the discontinuity network evolves separately.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
text:
From XFEM to XEFG
The next question was natural.
If enrichment can be added to finite element approximation spaces, can the same concept be used with meshfree approximations?
This led to work on the extended element-free Galerkin method (XEFG).
Meshfree methods already avoid fixed element connectivity and use domains of influence around particles. That gives them attractive properties for large deformation and evolving discontinuities, but traditional meshfree crack treatments also had difficulties, particularly near crack tips and in maintaining accurate discontinuous fields.
XEFG imports the partition-of-unity enrichment idea into the meshfree approximation.
The comparison is conceptually useful.






Figure 3: In XFEM, enrichment is associated with nodes of elements intersected by the crack. In XEFG, the same discontinuity concept acts through particle domains of influence. The meshfree support introduces additional geometric freedom, but also changes how the crack tip and partial support intersections must be handled. Adapted from Rabczuk and Zi (2007).



In the meshfree setting, the support of a particle may be fully cut, partially cut, or contain the crack tip.
That makes the kinematic problem somewhat different from the finite element case.
Our XEFG work addressed cohesive cracks in static and dynamic settings, later extending the concept to three-dimensional crack initiation, propagation, branching, and junction.
The physical problem remained the same.
The numerical representation changed.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: Why branch enrichment became an important issue
text:
Why branch enrichment became an important issue
Classical XFEM for linear elastic fracture mechanics often uses analytical near-tip branch functions motivated by the asymptotic crack-tip solution.
This can provide excellent accuracy when the asymptotic field is appropriate.
But cohesive fracture raises a different question.
If the crack-tip behavior is governed by a cohesive law rather than the classical traction-free LEFM singular field, should we always impose the classical branch enrichment?
Our work explored formulations in which cohesive cracks could be represented without conventional crack-tip branch enrichment.
That was not merely an attempt to shorten an equation.
It was an attempt to make the numerical representation more closely reflect the assumed fracture mechanics.
This distinction is important:

An enrichment function is not just a numerical trick. It is prior information inserted into the approximation space.

Therefore the enrichment should be compatible with the physics we are trying to represent.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: Three-dimensional fracture changes the difficulty again
text:
Three-dimensional fracture changes the difficulty again
A crack in two dimensions is represented by a line.
A crack in three dimensions is a surface bounded by a crack front.
That seemingly small change creates several major numerical problems.
The method must describe:

a moving surface,
a moving crack front,
local crack-front orientation,
propagation direction along that front,
curved surfaces,
branching surfaces,
and junctions between cracks.

Our later XEFG and partition-of-unity work placed significant emphasis on this three-dimensional problem.
The difficulty is not just computational cost.
It is geometric consistency.
A badly tracked crack surface can produce artificial kinks, discontinuous normals, or incorrect junction topology even if the underlying stress solution is otherwise accurate.
This is why three-dimensional computational fracture is partly a mechanics problem and partly a computational-geometry problem.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: Other representations emerged for good reasons
text:
Other representations emerged for good reasons
XFEM and XEFG were not the end of computational fracture.
Some later work in the uploaded collection explores related or alternative representations:

phantom-node methods,
cracking-particle approaches,
extended isogeometric formulations,
multiscale coupling,
peridynamics,
and phase-field fracture.

These approaches make different choices about where the discontinuity is represented.
A sharp enriched method says, in effect:
the crack is geometrically sharp
and the approximation is modified around it
A phase-field model says:
replace the sharp crack by a narrow continuous damage zone
Peridynamics reformulates the mechanics through nonlocal interactions so that bond failure can represent fracture without requiring the classical local PDE structure at the crack.
A phantom-node formulation represents separated material portions through overlapping element descriptions rather than explicit enrichment functions.
These are not merely competing numerical brands.
They are different answers to the same fundamental question:

How should a changing discontinuity be represented inside a numerical model?

That question is more fundamental than the name of the method.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
section: My computational-fracture work forms a sequence
text:
My computational-fracture work forms a sequence
Looking across the papers, I see a fairly clear progression.

1. Make arbitrary cracks independent of the mesh
Early XFEM work addressed cohesive crack tips, dynamic cracks, and multiple crack growth without remeshing.


2. Make the representation robust when cracks grow and interact
The work expanded to crack junctions, coalescence, dynamic propagation, and alternative tip treatments.


3. Move the enrichment idea into meshfree approximation
XEFG introduced discontinuous enrichment into element-free Galerkin approximations and developed it for static, dynamic, and three-dimensional cohesive fracture.


4. Extend the geometry and application domain
Later studies treated three-dimensional crack surfaces, reinforced concrete, shells, piezoelectric materials, and multiscale problems.


5. Explore alternative fracture representations
Phantom-node methods, cracking particles, peridynamics, and phase-field formulations reflect the broader evolution of computational fracture.
For this reason, I do not think my computational-fracture work should be compressed into a single article.
This article should serve as the entrance to a series.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
text:
Computational Fracture Series
This article is the gateway to a series on computational fracture. The first three articles are now available; the remaining articles are planned as the series develops.

Published
1. Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
This article. An overview of discontinuity, evolving geometry, remeshing, enrichment, and the progression from XFEM to XEFG and later fracture representations.
2. How Does XFEM Let a Crack Cut Through the Mesh?
How partition-of-unity enrichment gives the approximation the displacement jump and crack-tip kinematics that ordinary finite elements cannot represent.
3. Why Extend XFEM into a Meshfree Method?
How the same enrichment idea moves from finite elements to particle domains of influence, cohesive XEFG, and three-dimensional crack growth.
4. How Do Multiple Cracks Branch, Join, and Form a Fracture Network?
Multiple-crack growth, fatigue, crack competition, branching, coalescence, junctions, topology evolution, and three-dimensional crack tracking.


Coming next
5. Is Enrichment the Only Way to Represent a Crack?
Phantom-node methods, cracking-particle methods, peridynamics, phase-field fracture, and the trade-off between sharp and diffuse crack representations.
6. How Does Computational Fracture Move Across Scales and Structural Forms?
Reinforced concrete, piezoelectric materials, shells, multiscale coupling, atomistics, graphene, and nanocomposites.
7. What Did Enriched Methods Teach Us About Computational Mechanics?
A retrospective synthesis on approximation spaces, prior physical information, geometry-independent discretization, and what enrichment contributed beyond fracture.

Series principle: The mesh is only a numerical scaffold. The approximation should represent the mechanics.

title: Why Is Computational Fracture So Difficult?
text:
The broader mechanics lesson
The most interesting lesson from XFEM is not merely that cracks can be simulated without remeshing.
It is a more general computational-mechanics principle:

When the ordinary approximation cannot represent an important feature of the solution, enrich the approximation with the missing information rather than forcing the discretization to imitate the physics.

For fracture, the missing information is the discontinuity and, depending on the formulation, the crack-tip behavior.
For other problems, the missing information may be an interface, a singularity, a localized mode, or another known feature of the solution.
That is why the ideas developed in computational fracture have importance beyond fracture itself.
The mesh is only a numerical scaffold.
The approximation should represent the mechanics.

title: What Should We Teach Civil Engineers?
text:
English | 한글
I have been thinking about the civil engineering curriculum for a long time.
One question keeps coming back: What exactly are we trying to educate a civil engineer to do?
The question sounds simple, but it becomes difficult as soon as we look at a modern curriculum. Structural engineering, geotechnical engineering, water resources, transportation, environmental engineering, construction, sustainability, resilience, energy, data science, digital twins, and now AI all compete for limited space.
The usual response is to add another course.
That cannot continue indefinitely.
Before asking what new subject should be added, I think we need to ask a more fundamental question:
A useful place to begin is with a distinction that is sometimes blurred in everyday discussion.
Civil Engineering and Construction Engineering are not the same field.
Construction is essential to civil engineering. A bridge, tunnel, dam, or port that cannot actually be built has little engineering value. But construction is one part of a much broader discipline.
ASCE lists construction alongside transportation, coastal, structural, environmental, geotechnical, architectural engineering, engineering mechanics, and other civil engineering specialties. ABET makes the distinction even more explicit: its 2026–2027 criteria provide separate program criteria for Civil and Similarly Named Engineering Programs and Construction and Similarly Named Engineering Programs.
Civil Engineering is therefore not simply the engineering of construction. Its scope is much broader.
That distinction matters when we design a curriculum.

title: What Should We Teach Civil Engineers?
text:
Layer 1 — Mathematical and Scientific Foundation
This is the part of the curriculum that should remain deepest and most stable.



Area
Possible courses




Mathematics
Calculus I–II, Linear Algebra, Differential Equations


Probability
Probability and Statistics


Basic science
Physics, Chemistry


Computing foundation
Programming / Scientific Computing



Programming here does not mean learning a particular AI tool. It is better understood as a basic language for numerical methods, data analysis, simulation, and modern engineering computation.
The rise of AI does not make the fundamentals less important. If machines perform more of the calculation and information retrieval, the engineer becomes even more responsible for deciding whether the result is physically plausible.

title: What Should We Teach Civil Engineers?
text:
Layer 2 — Engineering Science
Engineering science provides a common language across civil engineering specialties.



Area
Possible courses




Solid mechanics
Statics, Dynamics, Mechanics of Materials


Fluid mechanics
Fluid Mechanics


Materials
Engineering Materials / Material Behavior


Computation
Numerical Methods, Computational Methods


Experiment
Experimental Methods / Measurement



One of the great achievements of the postwar engineering-science curriculum was to move transferable principles to the center of engineering education rather than teaching only procedures for particular structures or established designs.
That layer is not obsolete. What should change is that numerical and computational thinking should now be recognized more explicitly as part of modern engineering science.

title: What Should We Teach Civil Engineers?
text:
Layer 3 — Civil Infrastructure Systems
Civil engineering breadth has often been created by requiring introductory exposure to Structures, Geotechnical Engineering, Water Resources, Transportation, Environmental Engineering, and Construction.
The difficulty is that as the field expands, adding another small introductory course for every new area simply reproduces fragmentation inside the curriculum.
A different approach is to retain the disciplines but teach students more explicitly how they interact inside functioning infrastructure systems.







Infrastructure system
Examples of domains involved




Structural Systems
structures, loads, structural behavior


Ground and Underground Systems
soil, foundations, underground infrastructure


Water and Environmental Systems
hydraulics, hydrology, water, environment


Transportation and Urban Systems
transportation, mobility, urban infrastructure


Construction and Infrastructure Management
construction, cost, scheduling, safety, maintenance


Coastal and Energy Infrastructure
coastal systems, offshore structures, energy infrastructure



A city, for example, does not arrive divided into academic departments.
                     CITY / REGION
                          │
         ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
         │                │                │
       Water        Transportation       Energy
         │                │                │
        Dam ── River ── Bridge ── Tunnel ── Grid
                         │
                    Buildings
                         │
                  Underground
                         │
                 Waste / Environment
The purpose at this layer is not to teach every specialty in depth. It is to make students ask:

How do these subsystems connect to form a functioning infrastructure system?

title: What Should We Teach Civil Engineers?
text:
Layer 4 — Selected Professional Depth
Systems thinking alone is not enough. If integration is emphasized without depth, we simply create a different form of superficial education.
Every student should go deep enough in at least one area to calculate, model, analyze, and design real engineering problems.







Depth track
Examples of advanced courses




Structures and Mechanics
Structural Analysis, Reinforced Concrete, Steel Structures, FEM, Structural Dynamics


Geotechnical and Underground
Soil Mechanics, Foundation Engineering, Underground Engineering


Water and Environment
Hydrology, Hydraulic Engineering, Environmental Engineering


Transportation and Urban Systems
Transportation Engineering, Traffic Systems, Urban Infrastructure


Construction and Infrastructure Management
Construction Engineering, Project Management, Infrastructure Management


Coastal and Energy Infrastructure
Coastal Engineering, Offshore Engineering, Energy Infrastructure



These are implementation examples, not accreditation requirements. Universities can organize the tracks differently according to their mission, faculty, region, and students.
The principle matters more than the exact list.
Breadth allows an engineer to see the whole problem. Depth allows an engineer to actually solve part of it.
We cannot teach everything deeply. But we should not graduate students who have never gone deeply into anything.

title: What Should We Teach Civil Engineers?
text:
Layer 5 — Integrating Themes
This is perhaps the easiest layer to misunderstand.
If AI, energy, and climate matter, the immediate reaction is often to create a new vertical silo for each of them. I do not think that is the right architecture.







Theme
Examples of curriculum integration




AI and Data
sensing, prediction, surrogate modeling, SHM, digital twins


Energy
offshore wind, hydropower, nuclear infrastructure, energy storage


Climate
flooding, coastal hazards, adaptation


Sustainability
materials, life cycle, embodied carbon


Risk and Resilience
uncertainty, reliability, hazards, recovery


Digital Engineering
BIM, simulation, digital twins, automation



AI can appear in mechanics through computation and surrogate modeling, in structures through sensing and SHM, in surveying through spatial data and computer vision, and in construction through BIM and automation.
Energy similarly cuts across structural, geotechnical, hydraulic, coastal, and environmental engineering.
Layer 5 should therefore be understood as a horizontal mechanism for reconnecting established civil engineering knowledge to new societal and technological problems, not as another collection of stand-alone courses.
